title: Statistics I: Describing Data
learning_outcomes: Construct and interpret frequency distributions and basic descriptive summaries.
Calculate and distinguish mean, median, mode, range, variance, standard deviation and interquartile range.
Recognize skewness, outliers and the effect of data shape on summary selection.
Choose a defensible summary and visualization for common healthcare variables.

blocks.text: Descriptive statistics summarize the data actually observed. They help an analyst understand the centre, spread, shape and unusual values before comparing groups or fitting models. They do not, by themselves, prove causation or describe people who were not represented in the data.

rows: How often does each value or category occur?
Mean or median length of stay
Extreme length of stay or impossible age

blocks.text: A frequency table counts observations in each category or interval. Relative frequency is category count divided by the total valid count. A cumulative frequency adds counts up to and including the current ordered category; it is meaningful for ordered categories or numeric bins, not nominal labels.

Always state the unit of analysis. Twenty encounters may represent fewer than twenty unique patients if people can have repeated encounters. A patient-level percentage cannot be inferred from an encounter-level table without a defined patient-level method.

Consider a fictional set of five systolic blood pressure observations (mmHg): 118, 124, 126, 130, 152. These values are used only to teach arithmetic; they are not treatment thresholds or clinical guidance.

rows: No mode; all values occur once
Use only when weights and estimand are justified

blocks.text: The mean uses every value and is sensitive to extreme observations. The median is the middle ordered observation and is more resistant to extremes. The mode is most useful for identifying the most common category or repeated value; a dataset may have no mode or multiple modes.

blocks.label: Mean is not always typical
blocks.text: For skewed variables such as length of stay or charges, the median and IQR often describe the centre and spread more robustly. Report the distribution, not just a preferred statistic.

Dispersion describes how spread out observations are. Two groups can have the same mean but very different variability. The range uses only the minimum and maximum; the IQR describes the middle half; variance and standard deviation use distances from the mean.

rows: Total observed span; highly sensitive to extremes
Average squared deviation for the complete population
Unbiased estimator of population variance under standard sampling assumptions
Typical scale of deviations around the mean; same unit as data

blocks.text: For the five observations 118, 124, 126, 130, 152, the mean is 130. Deviations are −12, −6, −4, 0, +22; squared deviations sum to 144+36+16+0+484 = 680. Population variance = 680/5 = 136 mmHg² and population SD = √136 = 11.66 mmHg. Sample variance = 680/4 = 170 mmHg² and sample SD = √170 = 13.04 mmHg.

blocks.label: Quartile convention
blocks.text: Software packages can use different quartile algorithms, especially for small samples. State the method when exact quartiles matter; do not compare IQRs from incompatible definitions without checking.

A distribution describes how values are arranged. A symmetric distribution has similar tails on both sides of its centre. A right-skewed distribution has a long upper tail; a left-skewed distribution has a long lower tail. Multiple peaks may indicate subgroups, repeated processes or data issues.

rows: Mean and SD may be useful
A few large values pull the mean upward
Inspect median, IQR and upper tail
A few small values pull the mean downward
Inspect median, IQR and lower tail
Value unusually distant from most observations
Check source, units, eligibility and genuine variation

blocks.text: An outlier is not automatically an error. It may be a data-entry problem, unit mismatch, unusual but valid case, or signal of a distinct population. Never delete it solely because it changes the result. Document a defensible rule and, where useful, compare results with and without flagged observations.

blocks.label: Box-plot fences
blocks.text: A common exploratory rule flags values below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR. These are review flags, not proof of error and not universal clinical limits.

rows: Counts, percentages; median category when appropriate
Mean and SD, plus range or plot
Median and IQR, plus range or plot

blocks.text: A histogram groups numeric observations into bins; its appearance depends on bin width. A bar chart compares categories and normally has separated bars. A line chart connects values in a meaningful ordered sequence such as time. A chart title should name the measure, population and period; axes need units.

blocks.label: Do not hide the denominator
blocks.text: A percentage chart should disclose its denominator or sample size. Small groups can produce unstable percentages, and a visually large difference may represent only one or two observations.

exercises.question: For 2, 3, 3, 7, 10, calculate mean, median, mode and range.
exercises.answer: Mean = 25/5 = 5. Median = 3. Mode = 3. Range = 10 − 2 = 8.

exercises.question: A dataset has Q1 = 4 days and Q3 = 10 days. Calculate IQR and the upper 1.5×IQR review fence.
exercises.answer: IQR = 10 − 4 = 6 days. Upper fence = 10 + 1.5×6 = 19 days. Values above 19 days are exploratory flags for review, not automatic errors.

exercises.question: Why might median length of stay be more informative than mean length of stay?
exercises.answer: Length of stay is often right-skewed because a small number of very long admissions can pull the mean upward. Median and IQR are resistant to extreme values. Inspect the distribution and report both if useful.

exercises.question: A table shows 50 encounters from 35 unique patients. Can you say 50 patients were analyzed?
exercises.answer: No. The unit is encounter, and some patients contributed multiple encounters. State both counts and use a patient-level method if the question concerns patients.

exercises.question: What is the sample SD if the squared deviations from the sample mean sum to 80 across 9 observations?
exercises.answer: Sample variance = 80/(9−1) = 10. Sample SD = √10 ≈ 3.16 units. The denominator is n−1 for the usual sample variance estimator.

title: Statistics II: Probability and Sampling
learning_outcomes: Explain probability, complements, unions, intersections and conditional probability.
Apply Bayes' theorem to understand how prevalence affects predictive values.
Distinguish target populations, sampling frames, probability and non-probability samples.
Explain sampling variability, standard error and confidence intervals without common interpretation errors.
Identify selection, nonresponse, measurement and survivorship biases.

blocks.text: Probability quantifies uncertainty on a scale from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%). A probability of 0 means an event is impossible under the model; 1 means certain. Probability statements depend on the event definition, population, time horizon and assumptions.

rows: If an event has probability 0.12, its complement is 0.88
Subtract overlap so it is not counted twice
Both cannot occur in the same defined trial
Occurrence of one does not change probability of the other
Probability of A among cases where B is true

blocks.label: Independence is an assumption
blocks.text: Two events being different does not make them independent. In healthcare, age, disease status, treatment and outcomes are often associated.
Conditional probability changes the reference group. P(A|B) asks: among observations where B occurred, what fraction also had A? It is not the same as P(B|A).

Example: in a fictional cohort of 200 patients, 50 have a positive screening result and 30 of those have the target condition confirmed. The positive predictive value in this cohort is 30/50 = 60%. The denominator is all positive screens, not all patients with the condition.

Sensitivity and specificity describe test performance conditional on disease status in a defined study context. PPV and NPV describe the probability of disease status conditional on test result and depend strongly on prevalence in the tested population.
Bayes' theorem updates a prior probability using new evidence. In diagnostic testing, it explains why the same test can have different PPV in populations with different prevalence.

Worked example: assume a fictional test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%, and the target condition prevalence is 1% among 10,000 screened people. Expected condition-positive people = 100; true positives = 90. Among 9,900 without the condition, 5% test positive: 495 false positives. Total positive tests = 90 + 495 = 585. PPV = 90/585 = 15.38%.

blocks.label: Why this matters
blocks.text: A test with high sensitivity and specificity can still have a modest PPV when prevalence is low. Do not present sensitivity as the probability that a positive patient has the condition.

blocks.title: Interactive lab: screening-test predictive value
blocks.note: Enter prevalence, sensitivity and specificity as percentages. The result uses a hypothetical cohort of 100,000 and shows expected counts. Values are illustrative and are not a clinical test-performance estimate.

blocks.text: The target population is the group the research question aims to describe. The accessible population is the group practically reachable. A sampling frame is the operational list or mechanism from which units are selected. A sample is the subset actually observed.

rows: All eligible adult admissions in the defined hospital network during a year
Eligible admissions in participating sites with available records
Validated admission register for the study period
Admissions selected and included after applying the protocol
Admission, encounter, patient, prescription or laboratory result—must be explicit

blocks.text: A sample of 500 encounters does not necessarily represent 500 unique patients. Repeated admissions, missing records, exclusions and site coverage affect what the sample represents.

rows: Every frame unit has a known equal chance
Straightforward when a complete frame exists
Select every kth unit after a random start
Can improve representation of important strata
Select groups, then units within groups
Practical for dispersed populations; analysis must account for clustering
Fast but selection bias can be substantial
Include every eligible case encountered over a period
Often practical in clinical studies; still limited by site and period
Select cases for a defined reason
Useful for qualitative or specialized questions; not a probability sample

blocks.text: Selection bias occurs when inclusion is related to exposure, outcome or their causes in a way that distorts the relationship. Nonresponse bias occurs when participants who do not respond differ meaningfully from respondents. Measurement bias arises from systematic errors in how variables are captured.

blocks.label: Sample size does not cure bias
blocks.text: A very large convenience sample can estimate the wrong target quantity precisely. Representativeness and measurement quality matter alongside sample size.

A statistic such as a sample mean varies from sample to sample. Sampling variability is the natural variation caused by observing a sample rather than the entire target population. The standard error (SE) describes the estimated variability of a statistic across repeated samples under a specified sampling model.

For a sample mean under independent observations with finite variance, the familiar standard error is SE(mean) = s/√n, where s is sample SD and n is sample size. If s = 12 units and n = 36, SE = 12/6 = 2 units. This is not the same as the SD of individual observations.

For a sample proportion p, a common approximate standard error is √[p(1−p)/n], under conditions that make the approximation reasonable. Complex survey designs, clustering, weighting and finite-population corrections may require different methods.

blocks.label: Independence matters
blocks.text: Repeated measurements from the same patient are correlated. Treating them as independent can understate uncertainty. The analysis must respect the data structure.

A confidence interval is a range produced by a procedure that, under its assumptions, would cover the fixed population parameter at the stated long-run rate over repeated samples. A 95% confidence procedure has 95% coverage in repeated use when its assumptions hold.

A simple approximate interval for a mean in a sufficiently large sample is sample mean ± critical value × SE. For a 95% interval, a normal critical value of about 1.96 is sometimes used; smaller samples with approximately normal data and unknown population SD commonly use a t critical value. Proportions and complex designs need appropriate interval methods.

Example: mean = 130 units, SE = 2 units. Using 1.96 as an illustrative normal critical value gives 130 ± 3.92, or 126.08 to 133.92 units. This example is valid only if the normal approximation and underlying sampling assumptions are reasonable.

blocks.label: Correct interpretation
blocks.text: Do not say there is a 95% probability that this fixed parameter lies inside this already-calculated frequentist interval. The 95% refers to the long-run performance of the interval-generating procedure under its assumptions.

blocks.title: Interactive lab: approximate confidence interval for a mean
blocks.note: Uses mean ± 1.96 × (sample SD/√n), a normal approximation. This is not suitable for every sample or design; small samples may require a t critical value, and clustered or weighted data require design-aware methods.

Among 120 positive screens, 36 are confirmed cases. Calculate PPV in this sample.
exercises.answer: PPV = true positives/all positive tests = 36/120 = 0.30 = 30%. It is specific to this tested population and context.

exercises.question: A sample has SD 15 and n=25. Calculate the standard error of the mean under the usual independent-sample formula.
exercises.answer: SE = 15/√25 = 15/5 = 3 units. SD describes individual spread; SE describes estimated sampling variability of the mean.

exercises.question: Why can a very large convenience sample still be biased?
exercises.answer: Selection into the sample may systematically differ from the target population. Increasing sample size can reduce random error but does not remove systematic selection bias.

exercises.question: A 95% confidence interval is 12 to 18. Give a correct frequentist interpretation.

title: Statistics III: Statistical Inference
learning_outcomes: Formulate null and alternative hypotheses that match a defined estimand.
Interpret p-values, significance levels and confidence intervals correctly.
Distinguish statistical significance from clinical or operational importance.
Explain Type I error, Type II error, power, effect size and multiplicity.
Select a statistical test using outcome type, design, dependence and assumptions rather than a memorized shortcut.

blocks.text: Descriptive analysis summarizes observed data. Statistical inference uses a model and sample data to quantify uncertainty about a broader population or data-generating process. Inference depends on the sampling design, measurement quality, model assumptions and target question.

Before testing, define the estimand: the precise quantity the analysis aims to estimate, such as the difference in mean length of stay between two defined groups or the risk difference in a specified outcome by 30 days. A test cannot repair an unclear question or an invalid dataset.

The null hypothesis (H₀) is a reference claim used to calculate the distribution of a test statistic under a specified model. The alternative hypothesis (H₁ or Hₐ) describes departures of interest. Hypotheses should be written before examining results whenever possible.

rows: Is mean value different between groups?
H₀: μA − μB = 0; H₁: μA − μB ≠ 0
Is the event rate higher after a process change?
H₀: rate difference = 0; H₁: rate difference > 0, if a one-sided direction was justified in advance

blocks.label: One-sided tests
blocks.text: A one-sided alternative is not a way to obtain a smaller p-value after seeing the data. The direction and rationale must be specified in advance, and effects in the opposite direction remain important to report.

A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis and the statistical model are true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained, in the direction(s) defined by the test. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

rows: p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance H₀ is true.
Under H₀ and the model, data at least this extreme would occur with probability 0.03.
The data did not cross the chosen significance threshold; the estimate and uncertainty still matter.
p < 0.05 means the result is important.
Statistical evidence does not quantify clinical importance or implementation value by itself.
A smaller p-value means a larger effect.
P-values depend on effect, sample size, variability and model; effect size must be examined separately.

blocks.text: A p-value is conditional on the model and analysis choices. Data quality, missing-data handling, multiple testing, optional stopping and selective reporting can make a nominal p-value misleading.

The significance level α is a pre-specified long-run Type I error rate for a test under its assumptions. A common choice is 0.05, but it is not a universal law and should reflect context, consequences and analysis plan.

rows: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Probability of rejecting H₀ under a specified alternative and model
Magnitude of the difference or association, expressed on an interpretable scale

blocks.text: Power is not a property of sample size alone. It depends on the effect size of interest, variability, design, α, test choice, missingness and analysis. A study should be planned around a meaningful effect and feasible design, not an arbitrary target n alone.

sections.heading: 9.5 Confidence intervals, effect sizes and practical significance

blocks.text: A confidence interval presents an estimate together with uncertainty on the effect scale. It often communicates more than a p-value because it shows both direction and a range of values compatible with the model and data.

Example: an intervention group has a mean stay 0.8 days lower than a comparison group, with a 95% CI from 1.5 days lower to 0.1 days lower. The interval excludes zero under the stated method, but the practical importance depends on costs, patient experience, safety, baseline stay and implementation burden.

If an estimate is near zero with a wide interval, the study may be inconclusive. If an estimate is small with a narrow interval, it may be statistically distinguishable from zero but not important. If an estimate is large with a wide interval, it may be important but imprecise. Interpret the point estimate, interval and context together.

blocks.label: Do not equate non-significance with equivalence
blocks.text: To conclude equivalence or non-inferiority, use a design and margin specified for that purpose. A non-significant superiority test does not demonstrate that two interventions are equivalent.

Repeated measures, clustered observations, survey weights, missing data, small samples, non-normal residuals and confounding can change the appropriate method. When many hypotheses are tested, the chance of at least one false-positive result increases if each is judged at the same α without adjustment. The appropriate response depends on whether analyses are confirmatory or exploratory and on the decision context.

blocks.text: Do not report only significant subgroup results. Report the number of comparisons, pre-specified outcomes, analysis population and any adjustments.

blocks.text: Example reporting structure: “Among eligible encounters during the defined period, the estimated difference in mean length of stay was −0.8 days (95% CI −1.5 to −0.1; p = 0.03) using a two-group model. The estimate is an association in this observational comparison; residual confounding and selection bias may remain.” Replace this illustrative wording with the actual design-appropriate estimate and model.

Use the following sequence rather than selecting a test from a chart alone: (1) clarify the question and estimand; (2) identify the study design and sampling process; (3) identify outcome and predictor types; (4) determine whether observations are independent, paired or clustered; (5) inspect distributions, missingness and outliers; (6) choose a model that matches the design; (7) check assumptions and diagnostics; (8) report effect size and uncertainty; (9) interpret in context.

exercises.question: A test returns p = 0.02. Which interpretation is correct?
exercises.answer: If the null hypothesis and model assumptions are true, the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed, according to the test definition, is 0.02. It is not a 2% probability that the null is true.

exercises.question: A study reports p = 0.18. Has it proved there is no effect?
exercises.answer: No. It did not cross the chosen significance threshold. Examine the effect estimate and confidence interval; the study may be underpowered or imprecise. Absence of evidence is not proof of absence.

exercises.question: A result is statistically significant but the estimated reduction is 0.02 days. What else is needed?
exercises.answer: Assess the confidence interval, baseline context, measurement precision, patient and operational relevance, costs and implementation burden. Statistical significance alone does not establish practical importance.

exercises.question: Why is testing 40 outcomes at α=0.05 without disclosure problematic?
exercises.answer: Multiple testing increases the chance of false-positive findings across the family of tests. Pre-specify primary outcomes, report all comparisons and consider an appropriate multiplicity strategy.

exercises.question: A before-after study finds fewer readmissions after a new service. Can it conclude the service caused the reduction?
exercises.answer: Not by itself. Secular trends, case mix, coding, concurrent interventions, selection and regression to the mean may explain some or all of the change. The design and adjustment strategy determine causal strength.

blocks.text: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in specified populations and applies that knowledge to control health problems. For an analyst, epidemiology supplies disciplined definitions for who is counted, what event is counted, where and when it occurs, and what comparison is meaningful.

rows: Adults registered at a defined hospital during 2025
First confirmed diagnosis meeting a prespecified definition
When is the event or observation window?
A separate cohort or prior period with comparable definitions

blocks.label: Case definitions matter
blocks.text: Changing a case definition changes the numerator. A diagnosis code, a clinician-confirmed diagnosis and a positive screening result are not automatically equivalent.

Prevalence is the proportion of a defined population that has a condition at a specified point (point prevalence) or during a specified period (period prevalence). It measures the burden of existing disease, not the rate at which new cases develop.

Point prevalence = existing cases at a specified point ÷ population at that point. If 240 of 4,000 eligible residents have the condition on the census date, point prevalence = 240/4,000 = 0.06 = 6%. Period prevalence uses people who had the condition at any time in the defined period and a clearly defined population denominator.

rows: Proportion with condition at that point
People who had condition during period
Proportion affected at any time in period

blocks.label: Do not confuse prevalence and incidence
blocks.text: Prevalence includes existing cases. Incidence counts new cases among people at risk. Prevalence can be high because incidence is high, disease duration is long, or both.

sections.heading: 10.3 Incidence: new cases and time at risk

blocks.text: Cumulative incidence (risk) is the proportion of initially disease-free, at-risk people who develop the outcome during a specified follow-up period. Its denominator is the population at risk at the start, and its interpretation depends on the follow-up period and completeness.

Example: among 1,000 people free of the condition at baseline and followed for one year, 40 develop it. One-year cumulative incidence = 40/1,000 = 4%, assuming complete follow-up and a suitable closed-cohort definition.

Incidence rate (incidence density) uses person-time at risk: new cases ÷ total person-time contributed while participants are at risk. If 40 new cases occur over 2,500 person-years, the incidence rate is 16 per 1,000 person-years. Unlike cumulative incidence, the rate has a time dimension in its denominator.

rows: New cases ÷ at-risk population at baseline
Deaths ÷ population or person-time, as defined
Must state cause, period and denominator
Proportion of diagnosed cases who die over defined follow-up

blocks.label: Person-time is not simply headcount × nominal follow-up
blocks.text: People may enter late, leave early, die, be lost to follow-up or experience the outcome. Sum each person's eligible time at risk according to the protocol.

sections.heading: 10.4 Risk, odds and rate are different

blocks.text: Risk is a probability over a defined period. Odds compare the probability that an event occurs with the probability that it does not: odds = p/(1−p). A rate relates events to accumulated exposure time. They are not interchangeable.

rows: Cannot be calculated from risk alone without time/exposure information

blocks.text: An odds ratio compares odds between groups; a risk ratio compares risks. When outcomes are uncommon, an odds ratio may approximate a risk ratio, but the approximation worsens as outcomes become more common. In case-control studies, sampling is based on outcome status, so direct risk estimation is generally not available without additional information.

A screening test identifies people who may need further assessment; it does not by itself establish a diagnosis. Accuracy measures must be tied to a reference standard, threshold, population and clinical context.

rows: Among people with condition, what fraction test positive?
Among people without condition, what fraction test negative?
Among positive results, what fraction have condition?
Among negative results, what fraction do not have condition?
How much more likely is a positive result with condition than without?
How much does a negative result shift the odds?

blocks.text: Sensitivity and specificity are conditional on disease status. PPV and NPV are conditional on test result and change with prevalence in the tested population. Threshold changes commonly trade sensitivity against specificity. Verification bias, spectrum effects and an imperfect reference standard can also distort estimates.

blocks.label: Screening is not diagnosis
blocks.text: Do not label an individual as having a disease based only on a screening result. Clinical assessment and the appropriate confirmatory pathway are outside the scope of this analytics lesson.

Confounding occurs when the observed association between an exposure and outcome is distorted by a third variable related to both, and not on the causal pathway under the causal question. For example, age may be associated with both treatment selection and outcome, making an unadjusted treatment comparison misleading.

rows: A third factor distorts an exposure–outcome association
Consider age, severity and comorbidity; use design and justified adjustment
Inclusion depends on factors related to exposure/outcome
Only analyzing patients with complete follow-up may distort results
Effect differs across levels of another variable
Treatment association differs by prespecified age or severity strata

blocks.text: Effect modification is not simply a nuisance to remove. It may be an important finding to describe. Confounding control requires a causal rationale; indiscriminately adjusting for every available variable can introduce bias, including collider bias or adjustment for mediators.

blocks.label: Association is not causation
blocks.text: A statistical association can arise from causation, confounding, selection, measurement error, reverse causation or chance. Causal claims require a design and assumptions that support them.

sections.heading: 10.7 Ecological data and levels of analysis

blocks.text: An ecological analysis uses groups—such as districts, hospitals or countries—as the units of observation. An ecological association does not establish that the same relationship holds for individuals. Inferring individual behaviour from group averages is the ecological fallacy.

The reverse problem can also occur: individual-level associations do not necessarily describe group-level effects. Analysts should identify the unit of analysis, avoid mixing levels, and consider clustering when individuals are nested within wards, hospitals or regions.

items: Define the target population, case definition and study unit.
Set the time origin, observation window and follow-up rules.
Identify who is at risk at baseline and who contributes person-time.
Choose prevalence, risk, rate, odds or mortality measure based on the question.
Document censoring, competing events, losses and missing outcome status.
Describe screening reference standards and threshold selection.
Draw or articulate a causal model before choosing adjustment variables.
Report uncertainty, bias risks, generalizability and the exact denominator.

blocks.text: An epidemiologic measure is only as defensible as its operational definition. A clear formula does not compensate for an unclear population or inconsistent case ascertainment.

exercises.question: On a census date, 180 of 3,000 registered adults have a condition. Calculate point prevalence.
exercises.answer: 180/3,000 = 0.06 = 6%. The denominator must represent the population at the same defined date.

exercises.question: Among 800 people disease-free at baseline, 24 develop the condition over one year with complete follow-up. Calculate one-year cumulative incidence.
exercises.answer: 24/800 = 0.03 = 3% over one year. This is a risk, not an incidence rate.

exercises.question: There are 15 new cases over 1,500 person-years. Calculate the incidence rate per 1,000 person-years.
exercises.answer: 15/1,500 = 0.01 per person-year. Multiply by 1,000: 10 new cases per 1,000 person-years.

exercises.question: If risk is 0.25, calculate odds.
exercises.answer: Odds = p/(1−p) = 0.25/0.75 = 0.333, equivalent to 1:3. It is not 25%.

exercises.question: Why can PPV fall when prevalence falls, even if sensitivity and specificity stay the same?
exercises.answer: In a lower-prevalence population, there are fewer people with the condition. False positives among the much larger non-condition group can make up a greater share of all positive results, reducing PPV.

title: Research Methods and Evidence Appraisal
learning_outcomes: Distinguish major observational and experimental study designs.
Translate a broad topic into a focused, answerable research question.
Define protocol elements, population, exposure, comparator, outcomes and analysis population.
Recognize common threats to internal validity and generalizability.
Appraise evidence by examining methods, bias, precision, relevance and transparency.

sections.heading: 11.1 Start with a question, not a spreadsheet

blocks.text: Research begins with a decision-relevant question. A spreadsheet is a source of observations, not a research question. Before collecting or analyzing data, define what is to be estimated, for whom, over what period and under what comparison.

PICO is useful for intervention questions: Population, Intervention, Comparator and Outcome. PECO is often used for exposure questions. Descriptive questions may need a population, setting, variable and time period rather than a comparator.

rows: Adults admitted to a defined hospital

blocks.label: Make outcomes operational
blocks.text: “Improved care” is not an analyzable endpoint. Define the event, source, threshold, time window, unit and handling of missing or ambiguous records.

rows: Describes one or more cases without a comparison group
Can identify unusual signals and generate hypotheses
Exposure and outcome measured at a defined time or period
Useful for prevalence and service snapshots
Selects people by outcome status, then compares prior exposures
Efficient for rare outcomes or long latency
Selection and recall bias; direct risk estimation usually unavailable
Groups people by exposure and follows or reconstructs outcomes
Can estimate incidence and temporal sequence
Confounding, loss to follow-up and resource demands
Can balance known and unknown confounders on average
Evaluates an intervention without random assignment, often using comparison/time structure
Useful for real-world policy or service changes
Requires strong assumptions about counterfactual trends and confounding
Not designed to estimate population prevalence
Synthesizes eligible studies using explicit methods
Can summarize a body of evidence
Quality depends on included studies, search and synthesis choices

blocks.text: A design is not automatically high quality because it has a prestigious label. Execution, measurement, protocol adherence, missingness and analysis determine how much confidence is justified.

items: Background and rationale: why the question matters and what is already known.
Objectives and hypotheses: primary objective first; separate secondary and exploratory aims.
Design and setting: study type, sites, dates and workflow.
Population: inclusion/exclusion criteria and recruitment or sampling approach.
Exposure/intervention and comparator: operational definitions and timing.
Outcomes: primary/secondary endpoints, measurement source and time point.
Sample size rationale: target effect, variability/event rate, alpha, power and feasibility as applicable.
Data collection: instruments, source systems, training, validation and audit trail.
Statistical analysis plan: estimand, descriptive summaries, models, missing data, subgroup and sensitivity analyses.
Ethics and governance: approvals, consent or waiver, privacy, access control and retention.
Dissemination: reporting guideline, authorship and conflict-of-interest disclosure.

blocks.text: A protocol should distinguish confirmatory analyses from exploratory analyses. Changes after seeing outcome data should be documented with the reason, timing and impact on interpretation.

An outcome is a variable used to evaluate a health or service result. An endpoint is the operationalized outcome at a specified time or event. A surrogate endpoint is a substitute measure used in place of a direct clinical outcome; it may not reliably predict patient benefit.

rows: All-cause readmission within 30 days of discharge
Define eligible discharge, transfer handling and death
Documentation may differ from actual resolution
Components may differ in importance and frequency
Improvement may not translate into clinical benefit
Exclusions after randomization can break comparability
Analyze randomized participants in assigned groups
Requires careful handling of missing outcomes

blocks.text: Choose the primary endpoint before analysis and avoid switching it because another result looks more favorable. Define whether the unit is a patient, encounter, admission, prescription or event.

Internal validity asks whether the study estimate is credible for the study population under the design and assumptions. External validity (generalizability) asks how well findings apply to other populations, settings and times.

rows: Groups differ because of who enters or remains in study
Were inclusion, recruitment and follow-up comparable?
A third factor explains some observed association
Were important confounders identified using subject-matter reasoning?
Exposure or outcome measurement differs systematically
Were definitions, instruments and ascertainment consistent?
Loss to follow-up relates to prognosis or group
How many were lost, why, and how were missing outcomes handled?
Care or outcome assessment differs by group
Could participants, staff or assessors influence measurement?
Results are selectively published or reported
Is a protocol or registry available; are all outcomes shown?

blocks.label: Do not use a quality score mechanically
blocks.text: A checklist can structure appraisal, but a single total score can hide a fatal design flaw. Explain the specific risk and how it could change the estimate.

items: What exact question and estimand did the study address?
Does the design fit the question and establish the needed time sequence?
Was the population and setting clearly described?
Were exposure, comparator and outcomes measured validly and consistently?
Were important biases, confounding and missing data addressed?
Are estimates reported with uncertainty, not only p-values?
Do conclusions match the results and design, without causal overreach?
Are findings relevant to the intended population, workflow and decision?
Are protocol, analysis, funding and conflicts transparent?

blocks.text: Use design-specific appraisal tools and reporting guidance where appropriate. CONSORT supports transparent reporting of randomized trials; STROBE supports observational studies; PRISMA supports systematic reviews. Reporting checklists improve transparency but do not themselves guarantee good methods.

Evidence hierarchies are shorthand, not substitutes for appraisal. A well-conducted cohort may answer a prognosis or harm question better than an impractical trial; qualitative evidence may be essential for understanding acceptability and implementation. Match evidence to the question.

Consider magnitude, precision, consistency, directness, risk of bias, applicability, patient-important outcomes and feasibility. Statistical significance alone does not determine whether an intervention should be adopted.

exercises.question: Which design is generally suitable for estimating point prevalence in a defined population?
exercises.answer: A cross-sectional design can estimate point prevalence when the population, case definition and time point are clearly defined and the sampling/coverage process is appropriate.

exercises.question: A researcher selects patients with a rare adverse event and controls without it, then reviews prior exposure. What design is this?
exercises.answer: A case-control study. It can be efficient for rare outcomes, but selection and information bias need careful consideration; direct risk estimation is usually not available from the sampled case-control data alone.

exercises.question: Why should the primary endpoint be defined before examining results?
exercises.answer: Pre-specification reduces selective outcome switching and analytic flexibility, clarifies sample-size planning and makes confirmatory interpretation more credible.

exercises.question: A statistically significant observational association is described as proof that a medicine caused the outcome. What is wrong?
exercises.answer: Observational association can be affected by confounding, selection bias, measurement error, reverse causation and other explanations. The causal claim exceeds what the design alone establishes.

exercises.question: Name four items to inspect when appraising a study's missing data.
exercises.answer: Amount and pattern of missingness; reasons for missingness; differences between complete and incomplete cases; and whether the handling method and sensitivity analyses are justified.

title: Data Quality and Validation Foundations
learning_outcomes: Define core data-quality dimensions and explain why fitness-for-purpose matters.
Design field-level, record-level and dataset-level validation checks.
Distinguish missing, unknown, not applicable, not recorded and structurally absent values.
Identify duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent categories, temporal errors and referential-integrity failures.
Document data provenance, transformations, issue resolution and residual limitations.

sections.heading: 12.1 Data quality is fitness for purpose

blocks.text: Data quality is not a single score. Data are fit for a particular use when their limitations are understood and they are sufficiently suitable for the intended decision. A dataset can be adequate for monthly workload reporting but inadequate for estimating patient-level incidence.

rows: Percentage of eligible records with encounter date
Age within permitted range; valid date format
Values represent the real-world fact correctly
Compare a sample with an authoritative source
Entities or events are not unintentionally duplicated
Data are available when needed and current enough
Every encounter patient key matches a patient record
Origin and transformations can be traced
Source system, extract date, query version

blocks.label: Quality is contextual
blocks.text: A missing discharge date may be critical for length-of-stay analysis but irrelevant to a report that only counts admission volume. Define critical fields against the analytical purpose.

sections.heading: 12.2 Build a validation plan before analysis

items: Describe the business/clinical question and intended output.
Define dataset grain, population, fields and expected relationships.
Classify fields as required, conditionally required or optional.
Write allowed values, formats, ranges, units and temporal rules.
Specify duplicate rules and primary/foreign-key expectations.
Define missing-value semantics and acceptable missingness thresholds.
Decide which checks block release and which create warnings.
Assign owners, issue severity, remediation and sign-off responsibilities.

blocks.text: A validation rule should be testable, traceable and linked to a reason. “Check data quality” is not a reproducible rule. “Every non-null discharge timestamp must be at or after admission timestamp” is testable, although exceptions such as corrected records may require documented handling.

rows: Retain as unknown; do not invent a value
The field was not captured or entered
The concept does not apply to this record
The field does not exist for this source/version
Value withheld for privacy or policy

blocks.text: Missing completely at random, missing at random and missing not at random are statistical assumptions about missingness mechanisms, not labels that can be assigned by inspecting a single blank cell. The mechanism may be partly unknowable. Report missingness by important groups and assess sensitivity where it can affect conclusions.

blocks.label: Never silently convert blanks to zero
blocks.text: Zero is a value. Missing means no observed value. Replacing blanks with zero can create false averages, false event counts and misleading clinical interpretation.

rows: Age is numeric and within documented plausible bounds
Text in numeric field; impossible value
Discharge time is not earlier than admission time
Encounter ID is unique at encounter grain
Encounter patient key exists in patient table
Outcome date follows index date when required
Pregnancy-related field only applies to defined population/context
Monthly total reconciles to source report within tolerance

blocks.text: Plausibility ranges are not clinical reference ranges. A broad range can flag impossible values, but an extreme yet genuine observation should not be deleted. Clinical thresholds require the correct population, analyte, specimen, method and guideline context.

A primary key identifies a row at the declared grain. A patient key identifies a person; an encounter key identifies a care episode; a prescription key identifies a prescribing event. One patient can have many encounters, and one encounter can have many prescriptions.

A repeated patient ID is not automatically a duplicate. Duplicate detection must use the expected grain and business rules. Two identical-looking rows may represent two legitimate administrations, while two rows with different timestamps may still duplicate the same encounter.

blocks.label: Do not deduplicate blindly
blocks.text: Before removing records, identify the key, duplicate definition, source lineage and intended unit. Preserve a raw extract and document every deduplication rule.

Reconciliation compares analytical outputs with a trusted source or independent control total. Examples include row counts by month, totals by facility, counts of distinct patients, or a sample of records traced back to source screens under authorized access.

Provenance records where data came from, when they were extracted, which version or query was used, what transformations were applied, who approved access and what limitations remain. An analyst should be able to explain how a reported number was produced.

rows: System, table/report, owner and extract date
Cleaning, mapping, derivation and deduplication rules
Checks performed, results and unresolved exceptions
Reviewer, data owner or governance sign-off as required
Could invalidate a key result or expose sensitive data
Stop release; escalate to owner; correct and revalidate
Materially affects a major subgroup or measure
Resolve before publication or disclose with approval

blocks.text: A data-quality report should distinguish checks passed, checks failed, checks not run and checks not applicable. “No errors found” is not justified if checks were not designed or executed. Track issue owner, date, status, evidence and final disposition.

sections.heading: 12.8 Data quality mini-lab: audit a small extract

blocks.text: Use the supplied fictional encounter dataset from Chapter 5. Start by checking row count, distinct encounter identifiers, distinct patient identifiers, missing values by column, valid category values, duplicate keys and date ordering. Then compare key counts with the data dictionary and record exceptions.

items: Load the CSV without changing the original file.
Record row count and column names.
Check uniqueness at encounter grain and count distinct patient IDs.
Count missing values per field; distinguish expected from unexpected missingness.
Validate categories against the data dictionary.
Check admission/discharge date order and numeric units.
Write a short issue log with severity, owner and disposition.
Save a cleaned derivative separately and retain the raw extract.

exercises.question: A blank laboratory result is replaced with zero before calculating the mean. Why is this unsafe?
exercises.answer: Zero is a measured value, while blank indicates no observed value or another missingness state. The substitution changes the distribution and may materially bias the mean. Preserve missingness semantics and document handling.

exercises.question: A patient identifier appears 4 times in an encounter table. Are there 3 duplicate rows?
exercises.answer: Not necessarily. The table may have encounter grain, so one patient can have multiple valid encounters. Check encounter identifiers and the intended grain before deduplication.

exercises.question: Give a validation rule for admission and discharge timestamps.
exercises.answer: For records with both timestamps, discharge timestamp should be at or after admission timestamp, subject to documented exceptions such as corrected or transferred records. Record violations and investigate rather than silently deleting them.

exercises.question: What should a data provenance record include?
exercises.answer: At minimum: source system/table, extract date, population and period, filters/exclusions, transformation rules, validation results, versioned query or script, limitations and required approvals.

exercises.question: A dashboard total differs from the source system by 8%. What should the analyst do first?
exercises.answer: Do not force the totals to match. Compare population definitions, dates, filters, status rules, grain, refresh timing, duplicates and exclusions; trace a sample of records and document the reconciliation.

title: Healthcare Metrics and Indicators
learning_outcomes: Define a healthcare indicator with a precise numerator, denominator, population, period and unit.
Distinguish structure, process, outcome and balancing measures.
Calculate and interpret common quality, safety, utilization and operational indicators.
Stratify results responsibly while protecting privacy and avoiding misleading comparisons.
Create a metric specification sheet and communicate limitations.

sections.heading: 13.1 What makes a metric an indicator?

blocks.text: A metric is a quantified measure. An indicator is a measure selected to signal performance, quality, safety, burden or change against a defined purpose. A useful indicator has a clear specification, trustworthy source, accountable owner and an interpretation that supports action.

rows: What decision or process does it inform?
Exactly which events or records count?
Who or what was eligible to be counted?
Inclusion criteria, exclusions and unit of analysis
Calendar period, rolling window or event-based follow-up
Percent, rate, count, days; whether higher is better/worse
System, fields, extraction date and refresh frequency
Site, ward, age group or other approved subgroup
Accountable team, known caveats and action threshold if justified

blocks.label: A label is not a specification
blocks.text: “Readmission rate” is incomplete without defining readmission, index discharge, eligible population, follow-up window, exclusions and whether transfers or planned admissions count.

sections.heading: 13.2 Structure, process, outcome and balancing measures

rows: Availability of a clinical pharmacist on defined wards
Whether a care activity was performed
Eligible discharges with medication reconciliation documented
Unplanned readmission within a defined follow-up window
Discharge delay or staff workload after a reconciliation initiative

blocks.text: A process measure can improve without improving outcomes. An outcome can change for reasons outside the process being measured. Balancing measures help detect whether improving one target creates harm elsewhere. Use a coherent set rather than relying on one number.

rows: Eligible discharges with completed reconciliation ÷ eligible discharges × 100
Define completion and timing; count discharge or patient consistently
Define staffed/available beds and bed-day rules
Total inpatient days for completed discharges ÷ completed discharges
Define day-count convention, transfers and exclusions
Eligible index discharges followed by unplanned readmission within 30 days ÷ eligible index discharges × 100
Define index event, planned readmission and competing events
Reported errors ÷ defined exposure (e.g., administrations) × scale
Reporting is affected by reporting culture; not equal to true error incidence
Define start/end timestamps, units and outlier handling
People meeting defined vaccination status ÷ eligible population × 100
Define dose schedule, age and as-of date

blocks.text: Averages can hide variation. For length of stay, report median and IQR when skewed; consider stratifying by service and case mix. For rates, use exposure denominators when opportunities differ. For safety events, distinguish actual event incidence from voluntary reporting volume.

The denominator should represent the population with a genuine opportunity to experience or complete the event. Exclusions should be clinically or operationally justified and applied consistently. Avoid denominator changes that make performance appear better without improving care.

Example: 198 of 240 eligible discharges have documented reconciliation: 82.5%. If 20 additional discharges are excluded after review, the rate becomes 198/220 = 90.0%. That change is not a performance improvement; it is a denominator-definition change. Both the original and revised specifications should be documented and the impact explained.

blocks.label: Do not compare unlike denominators
blocks.text: A patient-level numerator over an encounter-level denominator, or events per admission compared with events per patient-day, creates a measure with a different meaning.

Stratification separates results by relevant groups, such as ward, facility, age band or service line. It can reveal unequal performance hidden by an overall average. Choose strata based on the question and a justified analysis plan, not only because a subgroup shows an interesting result.

Small denominators produce unstable percentages and can create re-identification risk. Apply organizational suppression rules and applicable privacy law. Avoid publishing small cells or combinations that could identify a patient. Do not interpret a small-group difference without uncertainty and context.

Risk adjustment may improve comparisons when patient mix differs, but it requires validated variables, an appropriate model, adequate data and transparent reporting. A risk-adjusted ranking is not automatically fair or causal.

sections.heading: 13.6 Run charts, control charts and targets

blocks.text: A run chart plots a measure over time to distinguish routine fluctuation from potential shifts or trends. A control chart adds statistically derived control limits based on a process model. Control limits describe process variation; they are not clinical targets, acceptable-risk thresholds or confidence intervals.

rows: Use consistent time intervals and definitions
Assess process stability and special-cause signals
Select chart type for data and subgroup structure
Compare performance with an explicit goal
A target is a policy or performance choice, not a statistical control limit
Compare with an external or peer reference
Ensure definitions, populations and periods are comparable

blocks.text: A monthly rate may fluctuate because of small denominators. Display numerator and denominator alongside the rate. Annotate policy changes, system migrations, staffing changes and other events that may affect measurement.

rows: Monitor reliability of a defined discharge process
Eligible discharges with documented reconciliation completed before physical discharge
All eligible completed discharges in participating adult medical wards during the period
Predefined categories where the process is not applicable; list exact codes and rationale
Calendar month, based on discharge date
Approved EHR discharge and reconciliation records
Check timestamp order, duplicate discharge keys, missing status and ward mapping
Ward and month; suppress small cells per policy
Documentation is a proxy for process completion; coding and workflow changes can affect capture

blocks.text: A metric dictionary is a governance artifact. It prevents different teams from using the same label for different calculations and makes trends reproducible.

items: Lead with the result and its defined population and period.
Show numerator, denominator, unit and trend.
Explain changes in case mix, eligibility, coding or source capture.
Distinguish observed performance from causal explanations.
Show uncertainty or small-number caveats where appropriate.
State whether a target or benchmark is locally defined or externally sourced.
Provide a practical next step and a named owner, not just a red/green label.

blocks.text: A dashboard should help users ask better questions. It should not hide denominator changes, missing data, suppression, refresh lag or limitations behind a polished visual.

blocks.text: Use synthetic data for Academy exercises. Do not place identifiable patient data in personal devices, public repositories, public AI services or unapproved cloud storage.

exercises.question: A ward completes reconciliation for 162 of 180 eligible discharges. Calculate the percentage.
exercises.answer: 162/180 × 100 = 90%. State that this is the percentage of eligible discharges, not necessarily unique patients.

exercises.question: Why should medication error reports per month not automatically be called the medication error rate?
exercises.answer: Reporting volume depends on reporting culture, awareness and systems, and may not equal actual event incidence. A rate needs a defined event and exposure denominator, such as administrations, with capture limitations explained.

exercises.question: Bed occupancy is 720 occupied bed-days and 900 available bed-days. Calculate occupancy.
exercises.answer: 720/900 × 100 = 80%, assuming available bed-days are correctly defined for the same wards and period.

exercises.question: A readmission metric improves after 15% of eligible discharges are newly excluded. What must be investigated?
exercises.answer: Determine why exclusions changed, whether the rule is clinically justified, applied consistently and specified before comparison. Recalculate using a consistent denominator and disclose the impact.

exercises.question: Why display numerator and denominator with a monthly percentage?
exercises.answer: The same percentage can arise from very different sample sizes and stability. Counts reveal the scale and help users interpret small-number volatility.

title: Learning Workflow and Professional Habits
learning_outcomes: Organize an analytical project so inputs, code, outputs and decisions are traceable.
Distinguish raw, intermediate and final data and preserve immutable source extracts.
Use documentation, data dictionaries, notebooks and version control concepts responsibly.
Plan work in small reproducible stages and validate each stage.
Communicate findings with clear limitations, handoffs and stakeholder-focused summaries.

blocks.text: A reproducible analysis is one where another authorized analyst can understand what was done, identify the inputs and methods, rerun the workflow in an appropriate environment, and explain the output. Reproducibility is a work habit, not a software brand.

The core chain is: question → approved data access → raw extract → validation → transformation → analysis → visualization → interpretation → review → release. Each stage should have a defined input, output and check.

rows: Population, unit, period and decision are explicit
Critical failures resolved or release blocked
Claims trace to evidence; reviewer signs off

blocks.text: A predictable folder structure reduces accidental overwrites and makes handoffs easier. Separate source data from derived data, code, documentation and outputs. Do not place identifiable patient data in a public repository, cloud folder or personal device without explicit authorization and approved controls.

rows: Restricted CSV or approved database extract

blocks.text: Use descriptive filenames with dates or version identifiers where appropriate, for example `2026-10_monthly_utilization_v01.csv`. Avoid names such as `final_final2_revised.xlsx`. Store sensitive data separately from code and documentation.

Raw data are preserved as received, subject to approved retention and access rules. Processed data are created through documented transformations. Outputs are tables, charts, models or reports. Never overwrite raw source data during cleaning.

rows: Read, checksum, document source; do not manually edit
Restricted access; immutable copy where policy permits
Transformation script and version; reproducible rules
Privacy review, quality sign-off and version label

blocks.label: Privacy by design
blocks.text: Use the minimum necessary data, approved environments, role-based access and secure transfer. De-identification reduces risk but does not guarantee anonymity. Follow institutional and legal governance requirements.

A README should explain project purpose, owner, data sources, date range, setup, run order, outputs, limitations and contact/approval route. A data dictionary defines fields, types, units, categories and missing-value semantics. A decision log records important changes and why they were made.

rows: Purpose, scope, setup, run instructions, outputs, owner, limitations
Field name, definition, type, unit, allowed values, source, missingness
Question, estimand, population, outcomes, methods, assumptions
Issue, severity, evidence, owner, status, resolution
Decision, date, rationale, alternatives and impact
Checks, expected result, observed result, pass/fail and reviewer

blocks.text: A notebook combines explanatory text, executable code, outputs and visualizations. It is useful for exploration, teaching and documented analysis. A script is better for repeatable tasks that should run consistently without manual cell execution. Mature projects often use both: notebooks for exploration and communication, scripts or tested functions for reusable transformations.

Notebook risks include hidden state, out-of-order execution, stale outputs, enormous embedded data and environment differences. Before sharing, restart the kernel and run all cells in order, remove sensitive outputs, record package versions and verify that paths are relative or documented.

items: Keep one analytical purpose per notebook.
Use descriptive section headings and explain why each step exists.
Separate configuration from logic where practical.
Avoid hard-coded secrets, passwords and access tokens.
Use fixed random seeds for reproducible simulation when appropriate.
Export final tables and figures from a documented run.
Convert repeated logic into tested functions or scripts.

blocks.text: Version control records changes to files over time and supports collaboration, review and rollback. Git is a distributed version-control system. A repository contains project files and history. A commit is a recorded snapshot with a message describing the change; a branch supports isolated work; a pull request or merge request supports review before integration.

rows: Keep code, documentation and non-sensitive sample data together
Small, coherent commits with meaningful messages
Use a branch for a feature or correction
Competing edits to the same content
Resolve deliberately and test after merge
Use approved organization and access controls

blocks.label: Never commit patient data or secrets
blocks.text: A private repository is not automatically an approved health-data environment. Do not push identifiable records, credentials, tokens, database dumps or restricted extracts to Git hosting.

Break work into small deliverables with acceptance criteria. “Analyze readmissions” is too broad. A workable sequence might be: approve cohort definition; validate discharge and readmission fields; produce monthly eligible counts; calculate 30-day outcome; reconcile sample records; draft interpretation; obtain review.

rows: Signed-off numerator, denominator, period and exclusions
Row count and unique key checks reconcile
Axes, units, denominators and period are explicit
Claims supported; limitations and privacy checked
Recipient can locate inputs, definitions, code and outputs

blocks.text: A handoff should include what was done, what changed, where files are stored, how to rerun, known issues, decisions needed and who owns the next action. Avoid relying on undocumented verbal explanations.

A concise analytical message answers: what question was asked, what was found, how certain or limited the result is, why it matters and what action is proposed. Separate observed facts from interpretation and recommendation.

Use an executive summary for the decision, a methods section for reproducibility, tables/charts for evidence and an appendix for detailed definitions. Avoid unexplained acronyms, misleading precision, overloaded charts and causal language unsupported by the design.

blocks.label: Analyst credibility
blocks.text: A transparent limitation is more useful than false certainty. Report data gaps, denominator changes, failed checks and uncertainty before stakeholders discover them.

sections.heading: 14.9 Volume 1 capstone: a small, auditable analysis

blocks.text: Capstone brief: using only the fictional Chapter 5 encounter dataset, produce a one-page descriptive report for a hypothetical quality team. Do not make clinical recommendations or infer causality.

items: Write a one-sentence question and define encounter as the unit.
Read the data dictionary and preserve the raw CSV unchanged.
Profile row count, unique keys, missingness and category values.
Calculate a descriptive summary for a selected variable, stating valid n and units.
Create one chart with a clear title, denominator and period if available.
Record at least three data-quality checks and their outcomes.
Write three findings, two limitations and one next analytical question.
Save the report, code/notebook, data dictionary and issue log in a structured project folder.

blocks.text: A successful capstone is not the one with the most charts. It is the one whose population, definitions, calculations, limitations and workflow can be inspected and reproduced.

blocks.text: This chapter's practical workflow is part of Foundational data work. The objective is to reproduce the same analytical result on both operating systems.

rows: Use your desktop file manager or terminal. In Bash/Zsh use `pwd`, `ls -la`, `mkdir -p academy-work`, and `cp source.csv academy-work/`. In Fish the same basic commands work; quote paths containing spaces.

Use File Explorer or PowerShell 7: `Get-Location`, `Get-ChildItem -Force`, `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force academy-work`, and `Copy-Item .\source.csv .\academy-work\`. Use `Get-Help` for command syntax.

blocks.text: Keep the same source file, folder structure and analysis definitions. Prefer CSV/UTF-8 for portable examples; check date formats, decimal separators and encoding when results differ.

exercises.question: Why should raw data be preserved separately from cleaned data?
exercises.answer: Preserving raw input provides traceability, allows transformations to be reproduced, supports audit and prevents accidental loss of source information. Cleaning should create a separate derived layer.

exercises.question: What is the main risk of running notebook cells out of order?
exercises.answer: Hidden state can cause outputs to depend on variables or transformations from earlier executions that are not visible in the current sequence. Restart the kernel and run all cells in order before sharing.

exercises.question: Can a private Git repository be used to store identifiable patient data?
exercises.answer: Not automatically. Repository privacy does not establish legal, institutional or security approval. Use only explicitly approved environments and never commit patient data or secrets without authorization and controls.

exercises.question: Write three acceptance criteria for a monthly readmission report.
exercises.answer: Example: (1) signed definition of eligible index discharges and 30-day unplanned readmission; (2) counts reconcile to the approved source and critical validation checks pass; (3) report displays numerator, denominator, period, limitations and reviewer approval.

exercises.question: What should a reproducible handoff include?
exercises.answer: Purpose and scope, source and extract details, data dictionary, transformation/analysis code, run instructions and environment, outputs, QA results, limitations, unresolved issues and next owner/action.

title: Spreadsheet Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain workbook, worksheet, cell, range, formula bar and ribbon concepts.
Enter, format and structure tabular data without damaging analytical meaning.
Use Excel Tables, sorting, filtering, freeze panes and data validation.
Distinguish values, formulas, displayed formats and stored data types.
Prepare a clean, auditable worksheet for healthcare analysis.

sections.heading: 1.1 The spreadsheet as an analytical workspace

blocks.text: A spreadsheet workbook is a file that can contain multiple worksheets. A worksheet is a grid of rows and columns. A cell is the intersection of a row and column, identified by an address such as B4. A range is a rectangular or otherwise specified collection of cells, such as A1:D20.

rows: Displays or edits the active cell content
Shows or navigates to a cell/range address

blocks.text: The ribbon organizes commands into tabs such as Home, Insert, Data, Formulas and View. Keyboard shortcuts differ between Excel, LibreOffice Calc and other spreadsheet applications. The concepts transfer, but verify the exact interface in your installed application.

sections.heading: 1.2 A good data table has a clear grain

blocks.text: Before entering or importing data, define what one row represents. This is the data grain. A table with one row per encounter should not also contain multiple medication records spread across repeating columns. Separate entities into separate tables when their relationships are one-to-many.
In this example, PatientID repeats because a patient can have multiple encounters. EncounterID is the likely unique key at encounter grain. Do not remove repeated patient IDs as duplicates.

blocks.label: Spreadsheet data layout
blocks.text: Use one header row, one observation per row, one variable per column, consistent data types within each column, and no merged cells or blank separator rows inside the data table.

Cell formatting changes how a value is displayed; it does not necessarily change the underlying value. A date may be stored as a serial number and displayed as 02-Jan-2026. A percentage format may display 0.25 as 25%. Formatting should clarify data, not conceal errors.

rows: Date serial under the spreadsheet date system
Numeric value with two displayed decimals
Leading zeros may be lost unless stored as text or formatted intentionally

blocks.text: Use numeric values for quantities, real date values for dates, and text for identifiers that are not used in arithmetic. Patient IDs, encounter IDs, postal codes and codes with leading zeros should usually be treated as identifiers/text, not quantities.

blocks.label: Do not use formatting as data cleaning
blocks.text: Changing a cell to date format cannot reliably repair text dates with ambiguous day/month order. Validate the source representation and parse dates explicitly.

Convert a contiguous data range into an Excel Table (often Ctrl+T in Excel). Tables provide structured headers, automatic expansion, filters and structured references. Give each table a meaningful name such as `tblEncounters`. Avoid duplicate or blank column headers.

Sorting changes row order; filtering hides rows that do not meet criteria. Both should be applied to the entire table, not a single column detached from its records. Before sorting, ensure the full dataset is selected or recognized as a table.

rows: Sorting one column alone can misalign records
Show selected wards, dates or statuses
Hidden rows can make copied totals incomplete
Wrong key selection can delete legitimate repeated events
Confirm whether visible rows only are included
Refer to table columns by name
Check table/column names when formulas are copied

blocks.label: Safe sorting habit
blocks.text: Click inside the table, use the table's sort command, and inspect several rows after sorting. Keep a raw source copy before making structural changes.

Freeze Panes keeps selected rows or columns visible while scrolling. Freeze the top row when headers are important; freeze both header rows and identifier columns when a wide dataset requires it. Data Validation can restrict entry to a list, date range, whole number or decimal rule.

Example: a Ward field may be restricted to MED, CARD, SURG and ICU using a controlled list. This prevents variations such as `Med`, `MED ` and `Medicine` from being entered inconsistently. Validation does not guarantee that imported data are valid; imported values still need checking.

Worksheet protection can reduce accidental edits to formulas or layouts. It is not a substitute for access control, encryption, approved storage or governance. Workbook passwords and hidden sheets should not be treated as secure protection for sensitive patient information.

items: Define the row grain and primary identifier.
Use one header row with unique, nonblank field names.
Keep one variable per column and one observation per row.
Store identifiers as text when leading zeros or exact characters matter.
Use consistent dates, units, categories and missing-value conventions.
Convert the range to a named Table where supported.
Validate imported values and check duplicate keys.
Keep raw data separate from cleaned or derived sheets.
Avoid merged cells, subtotals and notes inside the source table.
Document source, period, filters and transformations.

blocks.text: A well-structured table is easier to filter, calculate, query, import into Power Query and analyze with PivotTables. Good spreadsheet design is the foundation for later SQL and BI work.

exercises.question: A table contains 300 rows, with one row per encounter. A patient ID appears 12 times. Are these automatically duplicates?
exercises.answer: No. The grain is encounter, so a patient can have multiple encounters. Check the unique EncounterID key and the business definition of a duplicate.

exercises.question: An identifier 00042 displays as 42 after import. What likely happened and how should identifiers be handled?
exercises.answer: The spreadsheet inferred a numeric type and removed leading zeros. Import the identifier as text or apply a documented fixed-width text transformation; do not treat it as a quantity.

exercises.question: Why is sorting only the Ward column dangerous?
exercises.answer: It can separate ward values from the other fields in each record, corrupting row relationships. Sort the entire table or a correctly selected full range.

exercises.question: A cell displays 25% but its stored value is 0.25. Is that an error?
exercises.answer: Not necessarily. Percentage formatting displays the numeric proportion 0.25 as 25%. Check the intended meaning and formula, not only the display.

exercises.question: Name five features of a well-structured analytical worksheet.
exercises.answer: One header row; one variable per column; one observation per row; consistent data types; unique key at the declared grain; no merged cells or blank separator rows inside the table; documented units and missingness.

volume: Volume 2 · Excel, SQL and Healthcare Databases
title: Excel Formulas and Functions
learning_outcomes: Write formulas using arithmetic operators and relative, absolute and mixed references.
Use logical, conditional aggregation, text, date, lookup and statistical functions.
Understand formula errors, blank cells and calculation order.
Build auditable healthcare indicators using explicit denominators and criteria.
Test formulas with known examples and edge cases.

blocks.text: A formula begins with `=` and can contain constants, cell references, operators, functions and parentheses. For example, `=B2/C2` divides B2 by C2. Use parentheses to make intended order explicit: `=(B2-C2)/C2` calculates relative change.

Spreadsheet software follows an operator precedence order. Parentheses override the default order. For clinical or operational measures, label each component and test the formula on a small example whose answer you can calculate by hand.
When a formula is copied, a relative reference changes based on the new location. An absolute reference remains fixed using dollar signs. A mixed reference fixes either the column or the row.

headers: When copied one column right and one row down

blocks.text: Example: if B2 contains completed reconciliations and C2 contains eligible discharges, `=B2/C2` can be copied down. If a target percentage is stored in F1, compare with `$F$1` so the target does not move when the formula is copied.

blocks.label: Check locale separators
blocks.text: Some spreadsheet locales use semicolons rather than commas between function arguments. Function names and availability can also vary by Excel version and spreadsheet application.

rows: Return one value if condition is true, another if false
At least one condition is true
Sum values meeting one or more criteria

blocks.text: Use `IFERROR` carefully. It can hide a broken reference or invalid formula by replacing the error with a blank. Prefer to understand why the error occurred and use a fallback only when it is appropriate and documented.

rows: Remove leading/trailing and repeated ordinary spaces

blocks.text: A value that looks identical may contain a trailing space or non-breaking space. TRIM and CLEAN do not remove every Unicode whitespace character. Inspect suspicious values and use a controlled mapping rather than blindly replacing text.

rows: Build a date from year, month and day

blocks.text: Date arithmetic requires real date values and a defined time convention. For elapsed hours, subtract timestamps and multiply by 24 if the spreadsheet stores date-times as day fractions. Confirm time zones, daylight-saving rules where relevant, and whether endpoints are inclusive.

rows: Find a key and return a corresponding value
Look up in first column of a table and return a column to the right
Return relative position of a match

blocks.text: Exact match is usually required for identifiers. Approximate-match lookup is appropriate only for correctly sorted ranges and deliberate banding rules. Check duplicate keys in the lookup table: a lookup may return the first match and conceal a data-quality problem.

blocks.label: Version compatibility
blocks.text: XLOOKUP and dynamic-array functions may not exist in older Excel releases or some spreadsheet applications. Confirm target software before distributing a workbook; INDEX/MATCH may be more portable.

COUNT counts numeric values, while COUNTA counts non-empty cells. Text such as `N/A` is not a blank and can affect counts differently. Decide how missing values are represented before calculating denominators.

sections.heading: 2.8 Build and audit a healthcare indicator

blocks.text: Suppose a table `tblEncounters` contains one row per eligible discharge and a field `ReconciliationStatus`. A simple completion proportion could use `=COUNTIF(tblEncounters[ReconciliationStatus],"Completed")/COUNTA(tblEncounters[EncounterID])` only if every row is eligible and every EncounterID is valid and unique. If eligibility is represented in a separate `Eligible` field, use conditional counts for both numerator and denominator.

For example, numerator: `=COUNTIFS(tblEncounters[Eligible],"Yes",tblEncounters[ReconciliationStatus],"Completed")`. Denominator: `=COUNTIF(tblEncounters[Eligible],"Yes")`. Divide numerator by denominator and format as percentage. Check that the numerator is a subset of the denominator and that blank statuses are handled according to the metric specification.

blocks.label: Formula is not metric definition
blocks.text: A function can calculate a number, but it cannot decide eligibility, whether a blank means failure, or whether one row represents a patient or encounter. Define these rules first.

rows: Inspect denominator and define zero-denominator handling
Check spaces, type mismatch, key coverage and exact-match setting
Repair formula and inspect deleted/moved ranges
Check spelling, version and defined names
Wrong range, criteria, grain or hidden assumptions
Recalculate manually on a small sample; inspect formula references

Test a zero denominator and a blank value.
Test a missing lookup key and duplicate lookup key.
Test a boundary date and a value exactly at the threshold.
Copy the formula down and inspect reference movement.
Reconcile a sample of calculated rows independently.
