sections.heading: 4.1 Statistical significance is not clinical importance

blocks.text: A p-value measures how incompatible the observed data (or more extreme data) are with a specified statistical model and null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, the probability the result occurred by chance, or a measure of effect size.

Clinical importance depends on magnitude, patient relevance, harms, costs, baseline risk, uncertainty and context. A tiny effect can be statistically significant in a huge dataset; a clinically important estimate can be imprecise in a small study.

A 95% confidence interval is generated by a procedure that, under repeated sampling and model assumptions, covers the true parameter in 95% of repetitions. For a single interval, do not say there is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies inside it in the frequentist interpretation.
Interpret the estimate, interval width, null value and clinically meaningful thresholds together. Wide intervals indicate imprecision; narrow intervals can still be biased.

Subgroup analyses are vulnerable to low power, multiple testing and selective reporting. A significant result in one subgroup and a nonsignificant result in another does not prove that the subgroup effects differ. An interaction test evaluates evidence for effect variation, but still requires adequate power and prespecification.

items: Prioritise biologically/clinically justified subgroups.
Prespecify subgroup variables and interaction tests.
Report subgroup estimates and confidence intervals, not only p-values.
Avoid data-driven cut-points and overconfident claims.
Label exploratory analyses clearly.

sections.heading: 4.4 Communicate a result without overstating it

rows: Drug A is better because p=0.03.
The estimated mean difference was X units (95% CI Y to Z); interpretation is limited by the observational design and residual confounding.
The estimate was imprecise and compatible with effects from A to B; the study did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference.
At the prespecified threshold, sensitivity was X and specificity Y in this study population; predictive values will vary with prevalence.
The relative risk was 0.50; the absolute risk difference was X percentage points over the defined follow-up.

items: Question and population.
Design, setting, sample size and follow-up.
Primary outcome and exact operational definition.
Effect estimate with confidence interval and p-value where appropriate.
Clinical relevance, harms and absolute effects.
Risk of bias, missingness, generalisability and limitations.
Conclusion calibrated to design and uncertainty.

title: Reproducible research project
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply the core concepts of reproducible research project in a healthcare research context.
Define the population, unit of analysis, variables and estimand before selecting an analytic method.

blocks.text: A reproducible research project allows another analyst to understand the question, locate permitted source data, execute documented transformations, reproduce tables and figures, and inspect limitations. Reproducibility requires more than saving a script: it includes data provenance, versioned code, environment details, definitions, decisions and outputs.

items: Keep raw data immutable and separate from derived data.
Record source, extraction date, inclusion criteria and data dictionary.
Use scripts or queries rather than undocumented manual edits.
Set random seeds for stochastic procedures and record software/package versions.
Create a README with exact run instructions and expected outputs.
Do not include identifiable patient information in a portfolio repository.

blocks.text: Use the Volume 3 synthetic encounter dataset as the training source. A suitable question is: “How do encounter volume, missing discharge SBP and mean recorded discharge SBP vary across departments in this synthetic dataset?” This is a descriptive service-data exercise, not an evaluation of clinical effectiveness.

rows: All records in the supplied synthetic encounters file
Encounter count and SBP completeness by department
Mean and median recorded SBP by department
Unique encounter ID; department key match; valid SBP range review
Synthetic data; small counts; missingness; no causal inference

items: Load data and inspect shape, column types and duplicate encounter IDs.
Validate joins to department reference data and reconcile row counts.
Profile missing SBP by department; retain missing values rather than replacing with zero.
Calculate counts, nonmissing denominator, mean, median and missing percentage.
Produce a table and a clearly labelled chart with units and denominators.
Re-run from raw inputs and compare generated outputs with saved expected totals.

blocks.label: Expected validation anchors
blocks.text: The supplied synthetic file has 104 encounters, 60 distinct patients, 96 nonmissing SBP values and 8 missing SBP values. Department counts should sum to 104. These anchors validate file integrity, not clinical conclusions.

A concise report should contain a title, question, data and methods, results, interpretation, limitations and reproducibility notes. Include data cut-off and denominator definitions. A chart should not replace a table when exact values matter; a table should not replace a chart when pattern comparison matters.

Do not rank departments by mean SBP without considering case mix, measurement completeness, sample size and the synthetic nature of the data. Avoid implying that one department delivers better care from these summaries.

items: Include a README, data dictionary, analysis script/notebook, SQL reference, report and output figures/tables.
Use relative paths and a clean project structure.
Document setup and execution commands for a new machine.
Add tests for row counts, key uniqueness, joins and critical derived metrics.
Review for PHI, secrets, unsupported claims, broken links and licensing.
State what was not tested (for example, R or Quarto execution if unavailable).

blocks.text: A research question is a decision-focused statement that specifies a population, exposure or intervention, comparator, outcome and time horizon. A broad topic such as “hypertension treatment” is not yet analysable. “Among adults admitted with hypertension, is an ACE inhibitor-containing regimen associated with blood-pressure control at discharge compared with a calcium-channel-blocker regimen?” is more operational, although the observational design still cannot establish causality by itself.

rows: Sample, Phenomenon, Design, Evaluation, Research type

blocks.label: Operational rule
blocks.text: Each element must be definable in the data. If “control” has no threshold, measurement time or source, it is not yet a reproducible outcome.

An endpoint is the measured outcome used to answer the question. An estimand is the precise treatment-effect quantity the study intends to estimate, including population, treatment conditions, outcome variable, handling of intercurrent events and summary measure. In routine analytics, analysts often do not write a formal estimand, but they should still specify exactly what quantity a metric represents.

Do not silently substitute a convenient variable for the intended endpoint. A prescription for an antihypertensive is not proof of blood-pressure control; a diagnosis code is not necessarily a confirmed clinical diagnosis.

A statistical hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter. A two-sided test commonly evaluates H0: no difference against H1: a difference exists. Directional hypotheses should be justified before looking at results. The analysis plan records outcomes, predictors, populations, methods, assumptions, missing-data handling, subgroup analyses and reporting conventions.

items: Define the primary question and primary endpoint before inspecting outcome patterns.
Name the unit of analysis: patient, encounter, prescription, admission or measurement.
Specify how repeated records are handled; 3 encounters from one patient are not 3 independent people.
Predefine covariates using subject-matter reasoning rather than selecting them only because p<0.05.
Record planned deviations and distinguish prespecified from exploratory analyses.

blocks.label: Multiplicity
blocks.text: Testing many outcomes, subgroups and models increases the chance of at least one false-positive result. Prioritise a small number of prespecified primary analyses and label exploratory work.

Suppose a hospital dataset contains one index admission per patient, discharge SBP, age, diabetes status and antihypertensive class. A defensible question is: “Among adult inpatients with a documented hypertension diagnosis, what proportion have discharge SBP below the prespecified threshold, and how does this proportion vary by diabetes status?” This is descriptive/comparative, not automatically causal.

rows: Adults with eligible index admission and hypertension
Discharge SBP below the study threshold
Confounding, missing discharge readings and selection may distort comparison

blocks.text: A protocol should additionally specify exclusions, source tables, duplicate handling, implausible values, missingness, confidence intervals and the statistical test.

items: Changing the primary outcome after seeing which result is significant.
Using a patient-level denominator with an encounter-level numerator.
Defining control using a threshold that is inappropriate for the study population.
Treating an association as proof that one medicine caused better control.
Ignoring missing outcomes or excluding records without documenting why.
Reporting only p-values without effect size, confidence interval or clinical context.

blocks.text: A useful analyst habit is to create a one-page question specification before writing SQL or code. It acts as a contract between the clinical question, data extraction and statistical analysis.

sections.heading: 4.1 Study design determines what can be learned

blocks.text: Study design is the architecture that links participants, exposures, comparators, outcomes and time. The design determines temporality, susceptibility to bias, feasible analysis and the strength of inference. No statistical model can repair a fundamentally unsuitable design.

rows: Exposure and outcome measured at one time
Risk, rate, risk ratio, hazard ratio

blocks.text: A cross-sectional study estimates a snapshot, such as the proportion of clinic attendees with uncontrolled blood pressure during a defined month. It is useful for service planning but may not establish whether an exposure preceded an outcome.

A cohort study begins with exposure classification and follows participants for incident outcomes. A retrospective cohort uses existing records; a prospective cohort collects follow-up data forward. A case-control study samples people according to outcome status and compares prior exposures; it is efficient for rare outcomes but requires careful control selection.

blocks.label: Denominator discipline
blocks.text: In a cohort, risk is new cases divided by people at risk at baseline over a defined interval. In a cross-sectional study, prevalence is existing cases divided by the population assessed at a point or period. Do not call prevalence incidence.

Random allocation aims to balance known and unknown baseline confounders on average. Allocation concealment prevents foreknowledge of the next assignment; blinding reduces performance and ascertainment bias where feasible. Intention-to-treat analysis preserves the randomized comparison by analysing participants in assigned groups, subject to the trial's prespecified estimand and handling of missing outcomes.

items: Check random sequence generation and allocation concealment separately.
Review eligibility criteria and recruitment setting for external validity.
Inspect adherence, crossover, co-interventions and protocol deviations.
Distinguish efficacy under controlled conditions from effectiveness in routine care.
Read the protocol and statistical analysis plan when available.

sections.heading: 4.4 Registries, pragmatic studies and real-world data

blocks.text: Registries collect structured information about a defined population, condition, procedure or treatment. They can support surveillance and outcomes research but may have incomplete capture, nonstandard definitions and selection mechanisms. Pragmatic trials evaluate interventions in routine-care settings and often prioritise generalisability and implementation.

Electronic health records, claims, pharmacy dispensing and laboratory systems each represent different processes. A filled prescription is not identical to ingestion; a claim is not a complete clinical narrative; an absent code does not always mean absence of disease.

rows: What proportion of patients are controlled today?
Does baseline exposure precede incident disease?
Is a rare adverse event associated with prior drug exposure?
Does assigned treatment improve an endpoint?
How accurate is a screening test?
Compares index test with reference standard

blocks.text: The target population is the group to which the study intends to generalise. The source population is the group from which participants could be selected. The sampling frame is the operational list or mechanism used to identify eligible units. The analytic sample is the subset actually analysed. Differences between these groups create selection and generalisability concerns.

A hospital-based sample of admitted patients is not automatically representative of all people with hypertension in a city. Referral patterns, access to care, severity and admission criteria influence who appears in the dataset.

rows: Every eligible unit has known equal selection chance
Clear probability basis; needs a complete frame
Select every kth unit after random start
Sample groups such as hospitals or wards
Include every eligible case during a period

blocks.text: Probability sampling supports design-based inference when implemented correctly. Convenience and consecutive sampling can still produce useful service evaluations, but limitations must be explicit.

Sample size is driven by the primary estimand, expected variability or event frequency, desired precision or effect detection, type-I error, power, design and expected missingness/attrition. There is no universally correct sample size such as 30 or 100.

rows: Probability of detecting the specified effect if it is true under assumptions
Difference/association the study is designed to detect
Narrower intervals generally need larger N
Extra recruitment to account for unavailable outcomes

blocks.label: Interpretation
blocks.text: A nonsignificant result in a small study is not proof of no effect. It may be imprecise or underpowered. Report the estimate and confidence interval.

A service audit estimates the proportion of adults with controlled BP. If the expected proportion is 0.50 and the desired 95% margin of error is 0.10, a simple random-sample approximation is n = Z²p(1−p)/d² = 1.96²×0.5×0.5/0.1² ≈ 96. This is an illustration, not a universal recommendation.

If 10% of records are expected to be unusable, inflate to approximately 96/(1−0.10) = 107 records. A finite population correction, clustering, nonresponse patterns and the actual sampling design may change the required number.

items: Specify the primary outcome and calculation method before selecting N.
Use a validated sample-size procedure or statistician for comparative, clustered, repeated-measure or survival designs.
State all assumptions: expected event rate, variance, effect, alpha, power, allocation ratio and attrition.
Do not use post-hoc observed power as a substitute for interpreting the confidence interval.
Report the number screened, eligible, included, excluded and analysed, with reasons.

sections.heading: 4.1 Choose a test from the question and data structure

blocks.text: A statistical test is selected from the outcome type, number of groups, pairing/repeated structure, distribution, sample size and design. Start by identifying the unit of analysis and estimand. Do not choose a test solely because it is familiar or because software offers it.

rows: Within-person differences are the analysis units
Tests distribution/rank differences, not automatically medians
Expected cell counts and independent observations

blocks.text: An independent t-test compares group means. Welch's t-test does not require equal population variances and is often a sensible default for two independent groups. A paired t-test evaluates the mean within-person difference, not the two sets of observations as if independent.

Report group means and standard deviations, mean difference, 95% confidence interval and p-value. A confidence interval describes uncertainty under the model; it does not guarantee that 95% of individual values lie inside it.

One-way ANOVA tests whether all group means are equal under its model. A significant omnibus result indicates at least one difference but does not identify which groups differ. Planned contrasts or appropriately adjusted post-hoc comparisons are needed.

Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney methods compare rank distributions. They are not universal “median tests”; interpretation as a location/median difference requires additional distributional assumptions. Repeated measures require methods that account for within-person dependence.

Pearson chi-square compares observed and expected cell counts under independence. If expected counts are sparse, Fisher's exact test may be appropriate for a 2×2 table. For larger tables, exact or Monte Carlo approaches may be needed. Repeated observations from the same patient violate simple independence assumptions.

rows: Risk/prevalence difference or ratio; Cramér's V as relevant
Odds ratio and exact CI where appropriate

items: Inspect variable definitions, missingness, outliers and distribution.
Summarise each group before inferential testing.
Check independence, pairing and design effects.
Choose a test and document why it matches the estimand.
Estimate effect size and confidence interval.
Check assumptions and use robust/alternative methods when justified.
Report all planned analyses, not only significant results.

blocks.label: Common error
blocks.text: Do not run multiple pairwise tests after ANOVA without addressing multiplicity. Do not treat a p-value of 0.049 as fundamentally different from 0.051.

blocks.text: Regression models describe or estimate the relationship between an outcome and one or more predictors. The model form depends primarily on the outcome distribution and data-generating process. “Adjusting for everything available” is not a valid strategy; covariates should be selected from the question, design and causal structure.

rows: Expected mean difference per predictor unit
Odds ratio conditional on model covariates
Rate ratio with exposure-time offset when needed

blocks.text: A basic model is Y = β0 + β1X + ε. β1 is the expected difference in mean Y for a one-unit increase in X, conditional on other included predictors. For binary predictors, it is the adjusted mean difference relative to the reference group.

Assess linearity of the conditional mean, residual patterns, influential observations, heteroscedasticity and collinearity. Normality of residuals matters mainly for small-sample inferential calibration, not as a requirement that every predictor or outcome be normally distributed. Consider robust standard errors or transformations only with a clear rationale.

Logistic regression models log odds of a binary outcome. Exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio. An odds ratio of 1.5 means 50% higher odds, not necessarily 50% higher probability or risk. When outcomes are common, odds ratios can be substantially farther from 1 than risk ratios.

Report the reference category, adjusted odds ratio, confidence interval and absolute risks when possible. Assess linearity in the logit for continuous predictors, influential records, separation, calibration and discrimination. Avoid interpreting a model as causal without a defensible design and confounding strategy.

Poisson regression is commonly used for counts and assumes equality of conditional mean and variance. Overdispersion (variance greater than mean after conditioning) can make standard errors too small. Negative binomial regression adds a dispersion parameter. If follow-up time or population at risk differs, include an appropriate log exposure offset to model rates.
Check excess zeros, clustering, repeated measures and whether the count process is plausibly Poisson-like. A count of visits without a time-at-risk denominator may not be a fair rate comparison.

items: Define the outcome and target contrast before fitting the model.
Check sample size, events per parameter and sparse categories.
Inspect functional form, residuals, influence and collinearity as relevant.
Evaluate calibration as well as discrimination for prediction models.
Avoid automated stepwise selection as a substitute for subject-matter reasoning.
Report model specification, covariates, missing-data approach, diagnostics and validation.

blocks.label: Prediction versus explanation
blocks.text: A model that predicts well is not necessarily suitable for estimating a causal effect. A model with statistically significant coefficients is not automatically clinically useful.

blocks.text: Survival analysis studies time from a defined origin to an event. It handles right-censoring: a participant's event has not been observed by the last known follow-up. Censoring is not the same as a missing event date. Define time zero, event, censoring rule and follow-up window before analysis.

rows: Date of discharge or treatment initiation
No readmission recorded by day 30 or end of data capture
Eligible index discharges with defined follow-up

blocks.text: The Kaplan–Meier estimator estimates the probability of remaining event-free beyond time t, accounting for censoring under a non-informative censoring assumption. The curve steps down at event times; tick marks commonly indicate censored observations. The median survival time is the time at which estimated survival reaches 0.50, if it does.
The number at risk decreases over time. Late curve segments may be unstable when few participants remain. Always show numbers at risk and avoid over-interpreting tail behaviour.

The log-rank test compares event-time distributions between groups and is most sensitive when hazards are approximately proportional. The hazard is the instantaneous event rate among those still event-free at time t. A hazard ratio compares hazards, not cumulative risks or median survival times.

blocks.label: Hazard ratio caution
blocks.text: HR=0.70 is often described as a 30% lower instantaneous hazard under the model. It does not mean 30% fewer people experience the event over the full period.

The Cox model expresses the hazard as a baseline hazard multiplied by exp(βX). It estimates hazard ratios without specifying the baseline hazard. The proportional-hazards assumption means hazard ratios are constant over time for a predictor, conditional on the model.

Assess proportionality using graphical diagnostics and residual-based tests. If proportionality fails, consider time-varying effects, stratification or alternative models. Check influential observations, functional form and the adequacy of time origin and censoring.

items: Starting follow-up at different clinically meaningful points without defining a common time zero can create immortal-time bias.
Treating censored participants as event-free forever biases estimates.
Ignoring competing events can be misleading when another event prevents the event of interest.
Reporting only a hazard ratio hides absolute event-free probability.
Use a clear event definition, follow-up summary, curve, numbers at risk, effect estimate and confidence interval.

blocks.text: Diagnostic accuracy compares an index test with a reference standard in a defined population. The reference standard is the best available method for determining target condition status; it may itself be imperfect. Classify each participant as true positive, false positive, false negative or true negative.

Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN): the proportion of people with the condition who test positive. Specificity = TN/(TN+FP): the proportion without the condition who test negative. LR+ = sensitivity/(1−specificity); LR− = (1−sensitivity)/specificity. Likelihood ratios update pre-test odds to post-test odds.

rows: Among condition-positive people, how many test positive?
Among condition-negative people, how many test negative?
How much more likely is a positive result with disease?
Larger values provide stronger rule-in evidence
How much less likely is a negative result with disease?
Values nearer zero provide stronger rule-out evidence

blocks.text: PPV = TP/(TP+FP): probability of the condition among test-positive people. NPV = TN/(TN+FN): probability of no condition among test-negative people. Unlike sensitivity and specificity in idealised fixed-spectrum settings, predictive values change with prevalence and the population tested.

For example, a test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity has a PPV of about 50% when prevalence is 10%: among 1,000 people, 90 true positives and 90 false positives yield 90/(90+90). At 1% prevalence, PPV is about 8.3% (9 true positives, 99 false positives).

A receiver operating characteristic curve plots sensitivity against 1−specificity across thresholds. AUC measures ranking discrimination: the probability that a randomly selected case receives a higher score than a randomly selected non-case, under common interpretations. AUC does not establish calibration, clinical utility or fairness.

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies. A model can discriminate well but systematically overpredict risk. Evaluate calibration plots, calibration-in-the-large and slope where appropriate, and assess performance in the intended population.

items: Spectrum bias: test performance changes across severity, comorbidity or setting.
Verification bias: not everyone receives the reference standard, or verification depends on the index test.
Incorporation bias: the index test contributes to the reference diagnosis.
Threshold selection after inspecting data can exaggerate performance.
Report the tested population, setting, threshold, reference standard, 2×2 counts, estimates and confidence intervals.

blocks.text: Missing data are values not observed where a value would otherwise be expected. First distinguish structurally not applicable, not ordered, not recorded, unavailable, censored and data-entry failure. These states have different meanings and should not all be collapsed into one generic null.

rows: Missingness independent of observed and unobserved values
Random device failure unrelated to patient or measurement
Missingness explained by observed variables, conditional on them
Follow-up values more often absent in younger patients, and age is observed
Missingness depends on the unobserved value even after observed data
Very high readings are less likely to be documented

blocks.text: Create missingness counts and percentages by variable, time, site, department and clinically relevant groups. Look for patterns and process explanations. A missing BP may reflect workflow, acuity, device availability or documentation practice; it is not necessarily random.

items: Report the denominator for each variable and analysis.
Compare observed characteristics of records with and without the outcome.
Check whether missingness clusters by site, date, provider or system version.
Do not code missing values as zero or as normal.
Preserve source values and create explicit derived flags for missingness where useful.

blocks.text: Complete-case analysis excludes records missing any model variable. It is simple but may reduce precision and introduce bias unless assumptions are reasonable. Single imputation (such as replacing with the mean) generally understates uncertainty and can distort relationships.

Multiple imputation creates several plausible completed datasets, analyses each and combines estimates to account for within- and between-imputation uncertainty. It requires a defensible imputation model, inclusion of relevant predictors and careful treatment of outcome, design and missingness mechanisms. It does not magically solve MNAR.

Sensitivity analysis asks whether conclusions change under plausible alternative assumptions or analytic choices. Examples include complete-case versus multiple imputation under MAR, alternative outcome thresholds, plausible MNAR shifts, different covariate sets justified by design, and bounds for unobserved outcomes.

blocks.label: Do not hide the primary result
blocks.text: Prespecify the main approach where possible, report it first, and show sensitivity analyses as checks—not as a menu from which to select the most favourable result.

rows: Data dictionary distinguishes not applicable from unknown
Analysis method justified by estimand and assumptions
Sensitivity analyses where conclusions may depend on assumptions
Methods, amounts, assumptions and impact on estimates

blocks.text: Bias is systematic error in design, measurement, selection or analysis. Confounding occurs when a third variable is associated with both exposure and outcome and is not appropriately controlled, creating a distorted exposure–outcome association. Confounding is not the same as random error and is not reliably removed by increasing sample size.

rows: Only patients with complete follow-up are analysed, and follow-up relates to prognosis
Improve follow-up; describe selection; sensitivity analysis
Disease severity influences both treatment choice and outcome
Treatment association differs by age group
Report stratum-specific effects and interaction context

blocks.text: A confounder is a common cause of exposure and outcome. A mediator lies on a causal pathway from exposure to outcome. A collider is a common effect of two variables; conditioning on it can create a spurious association. Adjustment should be guided by a causal question, not by indiscriminately including every available variable.

For example, baseline severity may influence treatment selection and subsequent outcome, making it a potential confounder. A post-treatment laboratory response may be a mediator; adjusting for it can remove part of the total treatment effect.

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) represents assumed causal relationships with arrows. It helps identify minimally sufficient adjustment sets and avoid adjusting for mediators or colliders. A DAG encodes assumptions; it does not prove those assumptions from observed data.

Draw nodes for exposure, outcome, plausible common causes, mediators and selection variables. State the temporal order and explain why each arrow is plausible. Review with clinical or subject-matter experts.

A propensity score is the probability of receiving a particular exposure conditional on measured baseline covariates. Matching, weighting or stratification can improve measured covariate balance in observational comparisons. These methods do not control unmeasured confounding and depend on positivity, correct specification and appropriate diagnostics.

items: Define treatment strategies and baseline time zero.
Estimate propensity using pre-exposure covariates justified by the causal question.
Assess overlap and covariate balance; do not rely only on model discrimination.
Specify matching/weighting and handling of extreme weights.
Estimate outcomes using a design-appropriate approach and robust uncertainty.
Describe residual confounding and sensitivity limits.

blocks.text: Use “associated with” for observational associations unless the design and assumptions support stronger causal interpretation. Randomization strengthens causal inference but does not eliminate problems from nonadherence, missing outcomes, protocol deviations or poor implementation. Every causal claim depends on assumptions.

blocks.label: Reporting discipline
blocks.text: Separate what was observed, what the model estimated, what assumptions were required and what remains unknown.

blocks.text: A systematic review uses explicit, reproducible methods to identify, select, appraise and synthesise studies addressing a focused question. A meta-analysis statistically combines compatible study estimates. Not every systematic review should be pooled; clinical and methodological heterogeneity may make narrative synthesis more appropriate.

items: Register or publish a protocol where appropriate.
Define PICO/PECO, eligibility criteria, outcomes and study designs.
Search multiple relevant databases with reproducible strategies.
Deduplicate and screen records with documented reasons.
Extract prespecified data and assess risk of bias.
Synthesize transparently and assess certainty and applicability.

rows: Risk in exposed/intervention divided by comparator risk

blocks.text: Check which direction favours which group and whether estimates are on a ratio or difference scale. A ratio of 1 or a difference of 0 is the usual null value, but interpretation depends on the measure.

Statistical heterogeneity reflects variation in study estimates beyond sampling error. I² describes the proportion of observed variability attributed to heterogeneity under its assumptions; it is not a measure of clinical importance. Tau-squared estimates between-study variance on the chosen effect scale.

Fixed-effect models estimate a common underlying effect under their model. Random-effects models allow effects to vary across studies and estimate a mean of a distribution of effects. Random-effects pooling does not make incompatible studies comparable or remove bias.

A forest plot shows each study estimate and confidence interval, often with a pooled estimate. Inspect study weights, direction, interval width and heterogeneity. Funnel plot asymmetry may suggest small-study effects or publication bias, but can also arise from heterogeneity, chance or methodological differences.

Assess risk of bias at the study and outcome level. A precise pooled estimate from biased studies can still be misleading. Consider certainty frameworks and whether the evidence applies to the target healthcare setting.

items: Maintain a search log with database, date, exact query and limits.
Keep a record of duplicate removal and screening decisions.
Use a standard extraction form and verify key values against source reports.
Predefine effect measure, direction, model and heterogeneity plan.
Check conversions and avoid double-counting shared participants.
Report excluded full-text studies with reasons and all deviations from protocol.

blocks.text: Clinical trial data move from protocol and case report form (CRF) design through collection, validation, query resolution, coding, database lock, analysis and reporting. The analyst must understand the protocol, schedule of assessments, endpoint definitions, analysis populations and data-management plan before producing outputs.

rows: Can each endpoint and safety variable be captured unambiguously?
Are timestamps, units, visit windows and source documented?
Are range, consistency, missingness and cross-form checks defined?
Are discrepancies traceable and resolved without overwriting history?
Are outstanding queries, audit trail and freeze criteria satisfied?
Do datasets, derivations and outputs match the approved plan?

sections.heading: 4.2 CRFs, data dictionaries and edit checks

blocks.text: A CRF captures protocol-required information. A data dictionary defines variable names, labels, types, units, permissible values, origin and derivations. Edit checks identify missing, out-of-range or inconsistent values. Checks should flag records for review; they should not silently modify clinical source data.

items: Use stable subject and visit identifiers; avoid direct identifiers in analysis extracts.
Record units and reference ranges where relevant.
Distinguish not done, not applicable, unknown and pending.
Create cross-form checks, such as visit date after consent date.
Retain query status, resolution, user and timestamp in an audit trail.

blocks.text: Common analysis populations include intention-to-treat (ITT), modified ITT, per-protocol and safety populations. Exact definitions vary by protocol and must be prespecified. The safety population often includes participants who received at least one dose, but the protocol governs.

Endpoint derivations may require baseline selection, visit windows, repeated measurements, event adjudication and handling of intercurrent events. A derived endpoint should be traceable to source variables and a documented algorithm.

Adverse events require structured fields such as onset, end, severity, seriousness, relatedness, action taken and outcome. Seriousness is a regulatory classification and is not synonymous with severity. Drug exposure, concomitant medication and laboratory timelines are important for safety review.

blocks.label: Clinical boundary
blocks.text: The analyst supports data quality and summarisation. Causality, seriousness assessment and clinical decisions belong to appropriately qualified investigators/safety professionals under the applicable protocol and regulations.

rows: Eligible/enrolled per site and time interval
Screen failures divided by screened participants
Count or proportion, severity and denominator
Open queries grouped by elapsed days

blocks.text: Operational dashboards must distinguish counts from rates, use stable denominators and show data cut-off dates. A site with more queries may simply have more participants; normalise and contextualise before ranking.

sections.heading: 4.1 Statistical significance is not clinical importance

blocks.text: A p-value measures how incompatible the observed data (or more extreme data) are with a specified statistical model and null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, the probability the result occurred by chance, or a measure of effect size.

Clinical importance depends on magnitude, patient relevance, harms, costs, baseline risk, uncertainty and context. A tiny effect can be statistically significant in a huge dataset; a clinically important estimate can be imprecise in a small study.

A 95% confidence interval is generated by a procedure that, under repeated sampling and model assumptions, covers the true parameter in 95% of repetitions. For a single interval, do not say there is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies inside it in the frequentist interpretation.
Interpret the estimate, interval width, null value and clinically meaningful thresholds together. Wide intervals indicate imprecision; narrow intervals can still be biased.

Subgroup analyses are vulnerable to low power, multiple testing and selective reporting. A significant result in one subgroup and a nonsignificant result in another does not prove that the subgroup effects differ. An interaction test evaluates evidence for effect variation, but still requires adequate power and prespecification.

items: Prioritise biologically/clinically justified subgroups.
Prespecify subgroup variables and interaction tests.
Report subgroup estimates and confidence intervals, not only p-values.
Avoid data-driven cut-points and overconfident claims.
Label exploratory analyses clearly.

sections.heading: 4.4 Communicate a result without overstating it

rows: Drug A is better because p=0.03.
The estimated mean difference was X units (95% CI Y to Z); interpretation is limited by the observational design and residual confounding.
The estimate was imprecise and compatible with effects from A to B; the study did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference.
At the prespecified threshold, sensitivity was X and specificity Y in this study population; predictive values will vary with prevalence.
The relative risk was 0.50; the absolute risk difference was X percentage points over the defined follow-up.

items: Question and population.
Design, setting, sample size and follow-up.
Primary outcome and exact operational definition.
Effect estimate with confidence interval and p-value where appropriate.
Clinical relevance, harms and absolute effects.
Risk of bias, missingness, generalisability and limitations.
Conclusion calibrated to design and uncertainty.

blocks.text: A reproducible research project allows another analyst to understand the question, locate permitted source data, execute documented transformations, reproduce tables and figures, and inspect limitations. Reproducibility requires more than saving a script: it includes data provenance, versioned code, environment details, definitions, decisions and outputs.

items: Keep raw data immutable and separate from derived data.

blocks.label: Expected validation anchors

A concise report should contain a title, question, data and methods, results, interpretation, limitations and reproducibility notes. Include data cut-off and denominator definitions. A chart should not replace a table when exact values matter; a table should not replace a chart when pattern comparison matters.

Do not rank departments by mean SBP without considering case mix, measurement completeness, sample size and the synthetic nature of the data. Avoid implying that one department delivers better care from these summaries.

sections.heading: 5.1 Medication safety as a measurable system

blocks.text: Medication safety analytics examines risks across prescribing, dispensing, administration, monitoring and transitions of care. A medication error is not identical to an adverse drug reaction: an error is a preventable event that may or may not cause harm, while an adverse drug reaction is a harmful response to a medicine used at normal doses. Definitions and reporting rules must be taken from the applicable safety framework.

rows: An absent record may be a documentation gap
Alert firing does not prove exposure or harm
Incident report, clinical notes, laboratory timeline

blocks.text: An indicator should define an eligible population, numerator, denominator, observation period, exclusions, source and review process. For example, the proportion of eligible admissions with medication reconciliation completed within a defined interval requires a reliable admission timestamp, eligibility rule and completion timestamp.

items: Define the safety problem with pharmacists and clinical owners.
Identify the event and denominator at the correct grain.
Specify time windows and exclusions.
Validate whether source data capture the event consistently.
Review positive cases before labelling them errors.
Track balancing measures and unintended consequences.

blocks.text: High-alert medicines are medicines that bear a heightened risk of causing significant harm when used in error. Monitoring indicators may include required laboratory monitoring, dose verification, independent checks or documented counselling, depending on policy. A dashboard can identify missing documentation for review but cannot establish that a clinical action was not performed.

blocks.label: Interpretation limit
blocks.text: A missing monitoring record means the record is absent in the analysed source. It does not automatically prove that monitoring did not occur.

Incident reporting systems are designed to learn from safety events, near misses and hazards. Reporting rates are influenced by culture, ease of reporting, workload and policy. A rise in reports can reflect improved reporting rather than worsening safety. Use triangulation with audits, trigger tools and operational data where approved.
Classify incidents using the institution's approved taxonomy. Avoid ranking individual staff from raw report counts; such use can discourage reporting and misrepresent exposure to risk.

items: Use a stable operational definition before and after an intervention.
Choose an appropriate denominator and account for exposure volume.
Plot data over time and distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation.
Use balancing measures to detect unintended effects.
Document concurrent changes and case-mix shifts.
Escalate clinical interpretation and action to the authorised safety committee.

sections.heading: 6.1 BI turns operational data into decisions

blocks.text: Business intelligence (BI) is the governed process of turning operational data into information that supports decisions. It includes requirements, data integration, metric definitions, semantic models, visualisation, access control, refresh and ongoing support. A dashboard is one interface in that system, not the whole BI solution.

A good BI requirement starts with a decision: who needs to decide what, how often, at what level of detail, and what action follows? “Show all hospital data” is not a requirement. “Help the pharmacy manager identify stockout risk by item and site each morning” is closer to a usable requirement.

rows: Usable stock, average daily consumption, days of stock

blocks.text: A KPI needs a contract: name, purpose, formula, numerator, denominator, grain, filters, exclusions, time zone, source, refresh cadence, owner and known limitations. A semantic layer centralises business definitions so different reports do not calculate the same metric differently.

Separate additive measures (such as order-line counts) from semi-additive measures (such as end-of-day inventory) and non-additive measures (such as percentages and averages). Summing daily stock balances across days is usually meaningless.

blocks.label: Definition before visual
blocks.text: If two teams calculate readmission rate with different index-discharge rules, putting both values in the same dashboard does not make them comparable.

items: Identify users, decisions and the action that follows each metric.
Define use cases, grain, dimensions, measures and filters.
Agree on metric contracts and authoritative sources.
Prototype with representative users before polishing visuals.
Validate totals against source systems and existing reports.
Plan ownership, refresh, support, access and change control.

blocks.text: Capture non-functional requirements too: response time, data freshness, availability, accessibility, export needs, row-level permissions and auditability. A dashboard that is accurate but inaccessible to its intended users is not successful.

rows: Current ED waiting queue or pharmacy stock alerts
Service-line capacity, quality and financial trends

blocks.text: The same metric may need different aggregation, latency and access rules at different levels. Do not use a strategic monthly dashboard to manage a real-time emergency queue.

Measure adoption and decision quality, not just page views. Useful evaluation may include task completion time, report usage by intended roles, data freshness, metric disputes, action closure and user confidence. Avoid treating high usage as proof of value if users are forced to use the report.

blocks.label: Healthcare caution
blocks.text: A BI metric can influence staffing, funding or clinical operations. Validate definitions with clinical and operational owners and provide a correction/escalation route.

sections.heading: 6.1 Power BI Desktop, Service and architecture

blocks.text: Power BI is Microsoft's BI platform. Power BI Desktop is used to connect, transform, model and author reports; Power BI Service supports online workspaces, sharing, apps, refresh and governance subject to licensing and tenant configuration. Power BI Report Server is a separate on-premises option for eligible deployments.

rows: Windows desktop application; not natively supported on Linux
Availability and features depend on tenant, region and licence
Secure bridge for supported local data sources
Requires managed Windows host and administration

blocks.label: Your Linux workstation
blocks.text: CachyOS/Ryoku cannot run Power BI Desktop natively. Practical options include an authorised Windows PC, a properly licensed Windows VM if hardware and licensing permit, or a managed cloud/remote Windows environment. Use Linux-compatible BI tools for local hands-on work; do not assume the browser Service replaces Desktop authoring.

Import mode copies data into the Power BI model and supports fast interactive analysis, subject to refresh and model size. DirectQuery leaves data in the source and sends queries at interaction time, so performance depends on source design, network and query folding. Live connections use an existing semantic model or Analysis Services model with more limited local modelling options.

rows: Data freshness depends on refresh; model size
Source load, latency and feature limitations

blocks.text: Power Query is the data preparation layer used to connect, profile, clean and reshape data. Typical operations include setting types, renaming columns, filtering, splitting, merging, appending, grouping and pivoting. Steps should be named clearly and should preserve traceability.

items: Connect to a copy or approved source, not an uncontrolled PHI export.
Inspect column names, types, nulls, errors and distinct values.
Apply deterministic transformations with named steps.
Check query folding where supported and relevant.
Validate row counts and key uniqueness after joins.
Keep original source values where auditability requires them.

blocks.text: A useful first report has a defined audience, a small number of validated measures and a clear navigation structure. Start with a summary page, then provide detail pages for department, time and service where the questions justify them. Use slicers sparingly and label units, denominators and data dates.
A report page should not be filled with every available visual. Each visual should answer a question; remove charts that do not support a decision.

items: Publish only to an approved workspace and audience.
Confirm dataset/model permissions separately from report access.
Configure refresh credentials and gateway only through authorised administration.
Test row-level security using representative roles before release.
Document licence requirements, refresh schedule and support owner.
Never publish patient-level data to public workspaces or public sharing links.

blocks.text: A star schema organises measurable events in fact tables connected to descriptive dimension tables. A fact table stores events or periodic snapshots at a declared grain. Dimensions provide context such as date, department, medicine, patient cohort or site.

rows: Encounter key, patient key, date key, department key, LOS
One row per medication order line
Order key, encounter key, drug key, order date key, quantity
One row per standardised drug concept
Drug key, ingredient, ATC group, form

blocks.label: Grain rule
blocks.text: Do not put encounter, medication-order and laboratory-result facts into one wide table without understanding one-to-many multiplication. Separate facts can share conformed dimensions.

Relationships connect dimension keys to fact foreign keys. A typical star schema uses one-to-many relationships with dimensions filtering facts. Bidirectional filtering can create ambiguous paths and unexpected results; use it only when the model design requires and validates it.

items: Use stable surrogate keys where source identifiers can change or collide.
Define relationship cardinality and active/inactive status deliberately.
Avoid many-to-many relationships unless the business logic requires a bridge table.
Use role-playing date dimensions for admission, discharge and order dates where needed.
Validate totals before and after relationship changes.

blocks.text: DAX is the expression language used in Power BI models. Measures are evaluated in filter context: slicers, rows, columns and visual filters change the result. A measure is generally preferable to a calculated column for aggregations that should respond dynamically to report filters.

rows: Distinct encounters in current filter context

blocks.text: CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context. It is central to measures such as prior-period comparisons and filtered counts. Row context and filter context are different; context transition occurs in specific evaluation scenarios, including CALCULATE applied where row context exists.

Write simple measures first, validate against known SQL or spreadsheet totals, then add time intelligence and more complex context manipulation. Avoid copying DAX formulas without understanding their filter behaviour.

Time-intelligence calculations depend on a continuous, correctly related date table and clear definitions of calendar versus fiscal periods. Prior-year comparisons can be misleading if the data are incomplete, if the current period is partial or if the reporting calendar differs.

items: Mark and validate the date table as required by the model approach.
Check date relationships and missing calendar dates.
Compare DAX measures with independent SQL totals.
Test measures under single and multiple slicer selections.
Document how blanks, zero denominators and partial periods are handled.
Use explicit units and denominators in display labels.

blocks.text: Dashboard design starts with hierarchy: what must be noticed first, what context is needed and what detail is available on demand. Put the most decision-relevant validated measure in the primary visual area. Use consistent units, scales, labels and time windows.

items: Use titles that state the metric and population, not generic labels such as “Overview”.
Show data freshness and selected period visibly.
Use colour sparingly and never rely on colour alone to convey status.
Keep related measures together and align scales for comparisons.
Provide a path from summary to detail without overwhelming the first view.

blocks.text: Cross-filtering, highlighting, drill-down, drill-through, tooltips and bookmarks support exploration. Interactions should be predictable and should not silently change the denominator or metric definition. A tooltip can expose numerator, denominator, definition and source.
Test every slicer and interaction with realistic user tasks. Users should be able to return to a known state and understand which filters are active.

Accessible reports use readable typography, sufficient contrast, meaningful titles, keyboard navigation where supported, logical reading order, descriptive alt text and non-colour cues. Avoid dense layouts, tiny labels and red/green-only distinctions.
Test with users who have different screen sizes and levels of data literacy. A technically accurate report can still fail if labels, filters or interaction states are confusing.

Row-level security (RLS) restricts which rows a user can see, often through roles and identity-based filters. It is not a substitute for workspace permissions, source-system security, data minimisation or testing. Test with representative user identities and negative cases.

blocks.label: Security boundary
blocks.text: Never assume that hiding a page, visual or slicer protects underlying data. Validate model, workspace, export and underlying dataset permissions.

items: Document source owners, refresh cadence, credentials and failure notifications.
Validate refresh output and record last successful refresh time.
Use development/test/production workspaces where available.
Version metric definitions and change logs.
Assign report owner, backup owner and support route.
Review access periodically and retire stale reports.

rows: Use Git and native CLI tools. Docker Engine commands typically run as `docker ...`; check service state with `systemctl status docker` on systemd systems. Use Metabase/Superset or browser-based BI alternatives when Power BI Desktop is unavailable natively.

Use Git for Windows and PowerShell. Docker Desktop commonly uses its WSL 2 backend; start Docker Desktop and verify with `docker version` and `docker run hello-world`. Power BI Desktop is available on Windows; verify licensing and system requirements.

blocks.text: Container mounts, file permissions, service startup and networking differ. Use relative paths and document port mappings. Power BI Desktop is Windows-only; Linux alternatives are not feature-for-feature identical.

Verification on both systems: record OS version, shell, tool/database version, input file name and row count, key validation checks, output location and any differences. Use the chapter's stated learning outcome as the acceptance test.

sections.heading: 6.1 Tableau and the BI tool landscape

blocks.text: Tableau is a visual analytics platform with Desktop authoring and hosted or server-based sharing options depending on product and licence. Core concepts include data sources, worksheets, dashboards, stories, dimensions, measures, filters, marks and calculated fields.

The goal is not to learn every interface equally. Learn transferable BI concepts—data grain, dimensional models, metric contracts, chart selection, interaction, validation and governance—then develop depth in the tool used by target employers.

items: Connect to a supported file or database.
Inspect field roles and data types; distinguish dimensions from measures.
Build a worksheet with a clearly defined question.
Use filters and calculated fields only when their semantics are understood.
Combine worksheets into a dashboard with intentional layout and actions.
Validate totals against the source and document extract/live connection behaviour.

blocks.text: A discrete field creates categories or headers; a continuous field creates an axis. Incorrect field roles can produce misleading visual encodings.

sections.heading: 6.3 Compare tools for a Linux-first workflow

rows: Not native Linux; Windows environment required
Linux desktop authoring not generally available
Learn concepts using authorised Windows/macOS access or hosted options

blocks.label: Practical approach
blocks.text: Use Metabase or Superset for local Linux practice while learning Power BI concepts and DAX in a suitable Windows or managed environment. Tool availability, licensing and deployment requirements should be checked before committing.

Evaluate tools by total cost, user licensing, hosting, data connectors, semantic model, governance, accessibility, export, API and administration. A free authoring tool may still require paid hosting or enterprise capabilities. A portable SQL model and documented metric definitions reduce dependence on one visualisation tool.
Do not publish synthetic portfolio dashboards to a public service without checking the platform's terms and data exposure settings.

Record why the tool was selected and what trade-offs remain.

sections.heading: 6.1 ETL and ELT are pipeline patterns

blocks.text: ETL means extract, transform and load: data are transformed before loading into the target. ELT means extract, load and transform: raw or staged data are loaded first, then transformed in the target platform. Both need validation, lineage, access controls and failure handling.

rows: Connect, query, API pull, file ingestion
Land immutable source copy or raw batch

blocks.text: Batch pipelines process data at scheduled intervals. Streaming pipelines process events continuously or near real time. Incremental loading processes only new or changed records using a reliable watermark, change-data-capture mechanism or source timestamp. Late-arriving and corrected records require a policy.
A timestamp-only watermark can miss updates to old records if the source changes without updating the tracked field. Choose extraction logic based on source guarantees and validate completeness.

An idempotent pipeline can be run more than once without creating unintended duplicate effects. Use stable business keys, batch identifiers, merge/upsert logic and transaction boundaries. Retries should distinguish transient from permanent errors and avoid duplicating partially completed work.

items: Make each stage observable and independently testable.
Record run ID, start/end time, source range and row counts.
Retry transient network or service errors with bounded backoff.
Send permanent schema or validation failures to an exception path.
Support safe reruns and controlled backfills.
Alert an owner when freshness or completeness objectives are missed.

blocks.text: A data contract specifies expected fields, types, semantics, allowed values, ownership and change expectations. Schema drift can break pipelines or silently alter meaning. Use versioned schemas, compatibility checks and controlled migration.

blocks.label: Healthcare example
blocks.text: A laboratory source changing creatinine units or a medication code dictionary version can create a semantic break even if the CSV columns remain unchanged.

rows: Dates and values follow allowed rules
Loaded row counts and sums match controls
Latest available event is within agreed delay

blocks.text: A pipeline is not production-ready because it completed once. It needs repeatability, monitoring, controlled deployment, recovery and a named owner.

blocks.text: Online transaction processing (OLTP) systems support operational transactions with frequent inserts and updates. Online analytical processing (OLAP) systems support queries over historical, integrated and often aggregated data. Analytical workloads should generally avoid placing uncontrolled load on production clinical systems.

rows: Open data files plus table/transaction layers

blocks.text: Facts represent events or snapshots; dimensions provide descriptive context. Slowly changing dimensions (SCDs) preserve changes to attributes over time. Type 1 overwrites a value; Type 2 creates a new version with effective dates and a current-row indicator.

For healthcare, department names, provider affiliations, facility status and terminology mappings can change. Decide whether a report needs current labels or historically accurate labels at the time of the event.

Partitioning divides data into manageable segments, often by date or another frequently filtered attribute. Poor partition design creates too many small files or uneven workloads. Columnar formats such as Parquet can improve analytical scans by storing values by column and supporting compression and predicate pushdown.
CSV is convenient for exchange but weak for typed nested data, schema enforcement and efficient large-scale analytical reads. Choose a format based on scale, interoperability and governance.

rows: Original encounter extract with batch metadata
Standardised dates, keys, units and terminology
Department KPI mart or pharmacy utilisation fact

blocks.text: The medallion pattern is a useful organisation convention, not a guarantee of quality. Every layer needs data contracts, lineage, validation and retention rules.

items: Classify data before selecting storage location.
Encrypt in transit and at rest using managed controls.
Apply least-privilege access and separate duties.
Define retention, archival and deletion policies.
Monitor storage cost, query cost and data egress.
Test restore and disaster recovery for critical datasets.

sections.heading: 6.1 Git tracks changes, not data correctness

blocks.text: Git is a distributed version-control system for tracking changes to code and text-based project files. A repository records commits, branches and history. Git does not automatically validate an analysis or protect sensitive data; review and testing remain necessary.

items: Initialise a repository and add a descriptive README.
Use small commits with clear messages.
Create a branch for a focused change.
Review diffs before committing.
Merge through a reviewed pull request where possible.
Tag stable releases and document breaking changes.

blocks.text: A branch is an independent line of development. A merge integrates changes and may require conflict resolution when edits overlap. Resolve conflicts by understanding both versions, running tests and reviewing the final diff—not by blindly accepting one side.

For analytical work, keep code, SQL, documentation and synthetic sample data under version control. Large or sensitive production datasets should be stored under approved data-management controls, not committed to a public repository.

Issues track defects, questions and planned work. Pull requests provide a structured review of proposed changes. Reviewers should inspect logic, definitions, privacy, tests, documentation and reproducibility. A passing automated test does not prove that the clinical metric is correctly defined.

items: Describe the problem and expected behaviour in the issue.
Link code changes to the issue.
Include test evidence and output reconciliation.
Request clinical/domain review for definitions and terminology.
Record decisions and follow-up work.

blocks.text: Never commit API keys, passwords, tokens, private keys, patient identifiers or identifiable datasets. Use environment variables or a secrets manager, and add local secret files to .gitignore. If a secret is committed, revoke/rotate it; deleting the file in a later commit does not erase it from history.
Use a licence only when you have the rights to grant it. Document dataset provenance and usage restrictions.

A clean workflow separates raw inputs, transformations, tests, outputs and reports. Reproducible outputs should be generated by scripts or documented commands. For large binary files, consider approved large-file or artifact storage rather than forcing them into ordinary Git history.

blocks.text: A reviewer should be able to clone the repository, install dependencies, run documented commands and reproduce key outputs using the supplied synthetic data.

blocks.text: A shell interprets commands and connects tools through input/output streams. On your Fish-based Linux system, paths, quoting and environment-variable syntax differ slightly from Bash. Commands in this Academy should state the intended shell where syntax differs.

Absolute paths start from the filesystem root; relative paths are interpreted from the current directory. Linux permissions control read, write and execute access for owner, group and others. Processes can be inspected and stopped, but do not terminate services or processes without understanding their role.

items: Use quotes for paths containing spaces.
Inspect permissions with ls -l and change only what is required.
Use ps, top or btop to inspect processes.
Use Ctrl+C to interrupt a foreground command safely.
Avoid running downloaded scripts as root without inspecting them.
Do not use chmod 777 as a routine fix.

blocks.text: Pipes send one command's output to another command. Redirection writes output to a file or changes input. These tools enable repeatable inspection and automation without opening a GUI for every task.

Use project-specific environments to isolate Python and R dependencies. Record package versions and setup instructions. On Arch-based systems, use the system package manager for system packages and a deliberate project environment for Python libraries; avoid mixing package-manager ownership of the same files.
Fish environment activation differs from Bash. Follow the environment manager's Fish-specific setup instructions and verify the active interpreter with `which python` and `python --version`.

items: Use scripts for repeated tasks and keep them in version control.
Add error handling and clear exit codes.
Log actions without logging secrets or patient data.
Test on synthetic files before processing approved data.
Use backups before bulk renames or destructive changes.
Document scheduled tasks and the account under which they run.

blocks.text: A REST-style API exposes resources through HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. A response includes a status code, headers and often a JSON body. The API's documentation and contract define the supported behaviour; do not assume every service implements every method identically.

rows: Request correct permission; do not bypass

blocks.text: JSON represents objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null values. Nested responses require schema-aware parsing. APIs often paginate large result sets; follow the server-provided next link or cursor until completion and guard against loops or repeated pages.
Record extraction parameters, page counts, request time, response status and data cut-off. A successful first page is not proof that the full dataset was retrieved.

Common patterns include API keys, OAuth 2.0 access tokens and mutual TLS. Authentication establishes identity; authorisation determines permitted actions. Use least-privilege scopes and approved secret storage. Never hardcode credentials in notebooks or repositories.

blocks.label: Healthcare access
blocks.text: Only connect to approved systems for an authorised purpose. Do not test credentials or endpoints against a real patient system without permission.

Rate limits protect service availability. Respect documented quotas and Retry-After headers. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter; do not retry permanent validation or authorisation failures blindly. POST operations may not be safe to retry unless the API supports idempotency keys.
Use checkpoints and extraction manifests for long pulls. Validate record counts and duplicates after pagination.

items: Use TLS and validate certificates.
Store secrets outside source code and rotate them under policy.
Redact tokens and PHI from logs.
Validate response schema and content types.
Apply timeouts, bounded retries and pagination safeguards.
Record provenance and extraction time; follow retention and consent requirements.

blocks.text: A container image packages an application and its dependencies. A container is a running instance of an image with isolated processes, filesystem views and network configuration. Containers share the host kernel; they are not full virtual machines and are not a security boundary by themselves.

rows: Immutable build artifact made of layers
Running or stopped instance of an image
Persistent storage mounted into a container
Communication path between containers and host

blocks.text: A Dockerfile records build steps. Pin base-image versions and dependencies where feasible, use non-root users, minimise layers and avoid copying secrets into images. A reproducible build should specify inputs and produce a testable artifact.
For local analytics, containers can provide a consistent database, dashboard service or scheduled job environment. Keep source data in controlled mounts and make output locations explicit.

Volumes persist data beyond a container lifecycle. Bind mounts expose host paths to containers and require careful permission management. Compose defines services, networks, volumes and environment configuration for a multi-container application.

items: Persist database files in a named volume or approved mount.
Bind-mount only the project directories needed by the service.
Expose ports only to trusted interfaces where possible.
Use service names for internal Compose networking.
Back up and test restore for persistent data.
Avoid mounting the whole home directory into a container unnecessarily.

blocks.text: Containers can run with excessive privileges or expose sensitive mounts and ports. Use non-root execution, read-only filesystems where practical, minimal capabilities, image scanning and controlled secrets. Avoid privileged containers unless there is a documented operational requirement.

blocks.label: PHI warning
blocks.text: Do not put identifiable health data into a local container merely because it is isolated. The host, backups, logs, volumes and network remain within the security boundary and require approval.

A learning stack may include a database, a BI service and a one-shot ETL job. Each service needs health checks, persistent storage, environment variables and clear startup dependencies. Never use default credentials in a network-accessible production deployment.
On a 16 GB RAM laptop, keep the stack small, stop unused containers and monitor memory. A full enterprise data platform is unnecessary for foundational portfolio work.

blocks.text: Cloud computing provides on-demand compute, storage, networking and managed services. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) gives more control over virtual machines and networks; Platform as a Service (PaaS) manages more of the runtime; Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers a complete application. Responsibility is shared between provider and customer.

rows: OS, runtime, applications, data, identity configuration
Users, data governance and tenant configuration

blocks.text: Compute includes virtual machines, containers, serverless functions and managed runtimes. Storage includes object, block and file services. Networking includes virtual networks, subnets, routing, DNS, firewalls and private connectivity. Choose based on workload, security, availability and cost—not brand familiarity.
For healthcare data, network isolation, private endpoints, encryption, backup, recovery and identity controls are central design considerations.

Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls who or what can access cloud resources and what actions they may perform. Prefer role-based access, short-lived credentials, multifactor authentication and least privilege. Separate human identities, service identities and emergency access.

items: Use named individual accounts, not shared administrator accounts.
Grant only required permissions and scope them to resources.
Review access periodically and remove stale identities.
Enable audit logging for sensitive actions.
Protect root/owner accounts and recovery mechanisms.
Test access-denied cases as well as successful workflows.

blocks.text: Managed databases reduce routine administration but do not remove responsibility for schema design, query performance, backup policy, access, encryption and data governance. Logs and metrics support monitoring and incident response; avoid storing secrets or PHI in logs.
Define recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO) with service owners. Test restoration rather than assuming that a successful backup job guarantees recoverability.

items: Tag resources by project, owner and environment.
Set budgets, alerts and spending limits where available.
Stop or schedule non-production compute when idle.
Review storage retention and data-egress charges.
Use lifecycle policies and right-sized resources.
Understand provider and customer responsibilities for identity, data, configuration and endpoints.

blocks.text: Data governance assigns decision rights, ownership, definitions, access rules, retention and quality responsibilities. Data lineage records where data came from and how it changed. A catalogue helps users discover datasets, owners, definitions, sensitivity and approved use.
Governance is operational: it requires named owners, review cycles, issue escalation and change management. A policy document without implementation does not protect data.

rows: Required encounter ID is not null
Order ID appears once at order-line grain
Discharge date is not before admission date
Department code maps to approved reference
Sampled values reconcile to authoritative source

blocks.text: Data observability monitors quality and pipeline health over time. Track row counts, freshness, schema changes, null rates, distributions, duplicate rates, referential integrity and reconciliation. Thresholds should be contextual and owned.

A service-level agreement (SLA) defines service commitments. An operational level agreement (OLA) defines internal supporting commitments. A data freshness objective might require a dashboard to be updated by a specified time on business days; the exact threshold must match user need and source capability.

items: Detect and classify the incident by impact and urgency.
Notify the data owner and affected users using the agreed channel.
Preserve logs and batch metadata for investigation.
Identify root cause rather than only rerunning the failed job.
Correct data through a controlled, auditable process.
Record resolution, user impact and prevention actions.

blocks.text: Access reviews confirm that users still need their permissions and that roles remain appropriate. Health datasets may be subject to legal, contractual and institutional requirements. Apply purpose limitation, minimum necessary access, retention controls, approved transfer channels and audit logging.

blocks.label: Do not assume
blocks.text: Removing names does not guarantee anonymity. Rare diagnoses, dates, locations and linked records may still identify individuals.

A practical governance register records dataset, owner, steward, classification, permitted purposes, source, refresh, retention, quality checks, access groups, lineage and known issues. Review it when sources, definitions, regulations or organisational responsibilities change.
A data analyst should know when to stop work and escalate: unclear legal basis, unexpected identifiable data, unauthorised access, unexplained metric changes or suspected data breach.

sections.heading: 6.1 Production handoff is part of the deliverable

blocks.text: A production handoff transfers an analytical asset to its operational owner. It should explain what the solution does, how it is built, what data it uses, how it refreshes, how it is validated, who supports it and how it can be rolled back or retired.

rows: Purpose, architecture, setup, execution and contact
Version, changes, known issues and rollback

blocks.text: Use separate development, test and production environments where the platform supports them. Changes should be versioned, reviewed and tested before release. Avoid editing production reports or transformations directly without change control.

items: Commit code and definitions to version control.
Use synthetic or approved test data in development.
Run automated data and logic checks.
Obtain stakeholder sign-off on metric definitions and output.
Deploy using an approved process and record release version.
Keep a rollback or recovery procedure.

blocks.text: A runbook documents normal operation and response to common failures. Include data source dependencies, refresh time, expected row counts, validation steps, failure notification, retry rules, escalation contact and recovery procedure. Credentials should be managed by the organisation, not embedded in the document.
Document partial refresh and late-arriving data behaviour. A green refresh status does not prove that source data are complete or semantically correct.

Acceptance criteria should be agreed before delivery. They can include metric agreement, reconciled totals, role-based access tests, performance, accessibility, refresh success, documentation and user task completion. Capture known limitations and unresolved issues explicitly.
A stakeholder sign-off is evidence that the agreed scope was reviewed; it is not a guarantee that the system will remain correct after upstream changes.

items: Monitor adoption, freshness, failures and metric disputes.
Review access and ownership periodically.
Revalidate after source schema, terminology or policy changes.
Track enhancement requests and prioritise by decision impact.
Archive or retire duplicate and unused reports safely.
Preserve required records and communicate retirement to users.

Select a method appropriate to the question, data structure and intended use.
